Abstract: Analytical placers rely on differentiable objective functions to guide placement, typically combining intermediate surrogate metrics such as half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) and cell-density penalties. However, these placement-stage surrogates remain misaligned with downstream routed and timing quality. Prior work reduces this gap with human-designed terms or learned black-box surrogates, but the former requires expert retuning and the latter is difficult to explain, debug, or deploy in analytical placement flows. CoEvoP&R addresses these limitations with a large language model (LLM)-based framework that automatically evolves analytical placement objectives. At each generation, the prompt combines the restricted objective interface, baseline context, and archived prior candidates with routing-related feedback from placement, timing proxy, and routing tools. The LLM proposes readable differentiable objectives, which are embedded and validated in DREAMPlace, evaluated through a timing proxy and an actual router, and stored with their feedback to guide later generations. Across eight ChiP-Bench Nangate45 designs and three seeds, CoEvoP&R reduces post-route routed wirelength and congestion by 16.9% and 36.7%, with gains of 0.70 ns in worst negative slack and a 912 ns reduction in total negative slack magnitude over native DREAMPlace. Across eight ICCAD 2015 Superblue designs, it reduces post-route routed wirelength and congestion by 5.4% and 23.2%. Code is available at https://github.com/FCHXWH823/CoEvoP-R.git.

</details>


### [381] [Token-Level Cross-Modal Transformer with Contrastive Multi-Task Learning for Breast Cancer Subtype Classification and Survival Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16233)
*Suxing Liu Byungwon Min*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses challenges in cancer subtype classification and survival prediction by proposing a method to integrate various genomic and clinical data modalities more effectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to improve precision oncology by overcoming the limitations of current approaches that inadequately handle the integration of heterogeneous data for cancer analysis.

Method: The proposed method focuses on enabling fine-grained token-level interactions between modalities, structured token exchange for cross-modal fusion, and simultaneous optimization of survival and classification objectives to strengthen joint regularization.

Result: The new approach allows for better interoperability between different data modalities, enhancing both classification accuracy and survival predictions.

Conclusion: The integration of genomic and clinical data modalities using a more sophisticated approach can improve outcomes in cancer subtype classification and patient survival predictions.

Abstract: Integrating heterogeneous genomic and clinical modalities for joint cancer subtype classification and survival prediction remains a key challenge in precision oncology. Existing approaches suffer from three limitations: (1) they treat each modality as a monolithic feature vector, precluding fine-grained token-level interactions across modalities; (2) cross-modal fusion is typically performed through linear weighting or late averaging rather than structured token exchange; and (3) survival and classification objectives are optimized independently, missing a joint regularization signal.

</details>


### [382] [FIFA World Cup 2026 as a Contamination-Free Benchmark for LLM Forecasting Agents: Four Models, a Bookmaker, and 104 Matches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17765)
*Jiacheng Ding,Cong Guo,Jason Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The WC2026-Agents benchmark evaluates LLMs' forecasting abilities for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, contrasting their predictions with betting market data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess how well large language models can act as autonomous forecasting agents in predicting sports outcomes, specifically in a real-world context.

Method: Four advanced LLMs were tested on 104 World Cup matches, employing a search-act-reflect approach to predict match outcomes and evaluate their performance against the betting market.

Result: The LLMs had high prediction agreement but demonstrated varying decision-making effectiveness; none surpassed the betting market's performance as determined by Brier scores and returns.

Conclusion: The benchmark highlights key differences in model calibration, decision quality, and self-awareness despite similar prediction outcomes, emphasizing the need for comprehensive evaluation metrics.

Abstract: We introduce WC2026-Agents, a benchmark and dataset for evaluating large language models (LLMs) as autonomous forecasting agents on real, future events. For every one of the 104 matches of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, four frontier models -- Claude Opus 4.8, ChatGPT (GPT-5.5, high reasoning), Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Grok (Expert Mode) -- ran an identical search-act-reflect loop: gather evidence with a web tool, commit to a 1X2 (team-A win / draw / team-B win) distribution and a virtual 100-USD bet, and, after the match, reflect given only the final score. Because every match kicked off after the models' training cutoffs, the benchmark is contamination-free by construction. Crucially, we pair the four agents with a fifth competitor drawn from the same information environment -- the pre-match betting market -- collected as per-match 1X2 odds, giving an economically grounded baseline and letting us score not just what an agent predicts but what it does with money. The release contains 416 forecasts and 414 reflections with verbatim reasoning, ground truth (including penalty shootouts), odds, and a reproducible evaluation suite. A reference evaluation surfaces findings that raw accuracy hides: the four agents issue an identical top pick in 92% of matches and none beats the market's Brier score; indeed, a naive flat stake on the market favorite out-earns all four agents. Yet the agents diverge sharply as decision-makers: betting return-on-investment ranges from -18% to +10%, fading the market is unprofitable for all four, the share of forecasts that cite the market ranges from 12% to 100%, and self-reported error rates on wrong picks range from 36% to 86%. The benchmark thus measures calibration, decision quality, and self-knowledge -- axes on which frontier models differ even when their predictions do not. Data and code: https://github.com/graphuofm/FIFA2026LLM

</details>


### [383] [HantaWatch: Federated Learning for Hantavirus Genomic Surveillance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16234)
*Shanika Iroshi Nanayakkara,Shiva Raj Pokhrel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HantaWatch is a federated learning framework for Hantavirus genomic surveillance that allows collaborative training without sharing raw data, enhancing predictive performance and expert review prioritization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation behind this paper is to address the challenges of limited sequence data, source heterogeneity, and expert capacity in Hantavirus genomic surveillance.

Method: The method involves a federated learning framework incorporating features such as k-mer extraction, adaptive optimization, and specific model selection, allowing laboratories to collaborate while protecting data privacy.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that HantaWatch facilitates high-risk screening, clinical and outbreak prediction, and classification tasks, achieving a balance between performance and risk.

Conclusion: HantaWatch enables effective decentralized Hantavirus surveillance by converting model outputs into actionable insights while maintaining necessary expert oversight.

Abstract: Hantavirus genomic surveillance is limited by the distribution of sequence data, non-IID source heterogeneity, and constrained expert-review capacity. We propose HantaWatch, a federated learning framework that enables laboratories and surveillance sites to collaboratively train sequence-based models without sharing raw data. HantaWatch integrates k-mer feature extraction, source-aware federated client construction, adaptive DU-FedProx optimization, surveillance-specific model selection, and prediction-only triage. Experiments on binary and multi-class tasks show that HantaWatch supports high-risk screening, outbreak-associated prediction, clade classification, and clinical-syndrome categorization while balancing predictive performance, false-negative risk, and update stability. The framework converts model output into risk scores, confidence estimates, uncertainty flags, and ranked expert-review priorities. HantaWatch therefore provides a practical federated decision-support layer for decentralized Hantavirus surveillance, supporting expert prioritization without replacing laboratory or public-health interpretation.

</details>


### [384] [OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16235)
*Narayan Schuetz,Yuze Bai,Lianggang Pan,Edgar Eggert,Favour Nerrise,Juan Delgado-SanMartin,Max Rosenblattl,Milana Gurbanova,Mohammad Asadi,Anders Johnson,Paul Schmiedmayer,Dennis Wang,Allan Lawrie,Daniel Seung Kim,Xin Liu,Akshay Paruchuri,Ehsan Adeli,Euan Ashley,Kelly W. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Release of OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest open-access wearable health dataset with over 60 million hours of data from various sensors, aimed at democratizing wearable health AI research through open-source models and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To accelerate open science in wearable health by providing access to large datasets and models that are typically not publicly available, facilitating research in health monitoring and AI.

Method: Release of the OpenMHC dataset derived from a decade of My Heart Counts study data, along with open-source implementations of foundation models and a unified benchmark for comparative analysis across multiple predictive tracks.

Result: OpenMHC includes >60 million hours of data from 19 sensor channels and 169 variables, offering comprehensive insights into health behaviors and metrics, with a benchmark for evaluating different health AI models.

Conclusion: By promoting open-access resources in wearable health research, we aim to enable researchers and the community to advance the field collaboratively.

Abstract: Mobile and wearable devices offer an unprecedented opportunity for continuous, passive health monitoring and active health coaching. However, the largest wearable datasets are not publicly available for research, and leading wearable foundation models trained on such datasets are rarely open-weight or come with reproducible training code. To accelerate open science in wearable health, we release OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest and most comprehensive open-access wearable health dataset to date, alongside open-source implementations of recent wearable foundation models. OpenMHC, derived from over a decade of data collected through the My Heart Counts study app, includes >60 million hours of wearable data across 19 sensor channels (e.g., step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts) and up to 169 linked variables, including health, lifestyle, mood, and behavior from 11,894 consenting participants. Furthermore, we introduce a unified, open benchmark that enables standardized comparison of wearable health models across three tracks: health and behavior downstream prediction, multivariate data imputation, and time-series forecasting. We benchmark classical methods alongside recent wearable and multivariate time series foundation models. By open-sourcing data, code, and model weights at this unprecedented scale, we aim to democratize wearable health AI research and enable the community to drive open progress in this domain.

</details>


### [385] [The Failures of Marginal Influence-Based Attribution Methods for Global Time Series Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16236)
*Amadeo Tunyi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Current explainability methods for time series models yield inadequate attribution scores due to a fundamental computational mismatch regarding temporal dependencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the limitations of existing explainability methods for time series models, particularly in how they attribute influence over time.

Method: The authors analyze existing methods for computing attribution scores, such as marginal conditioning and off-manifold gradients, highlighting their failure to account for temporal dependencies correctly.

Result: They find that standard attribution methods, like SHAP, fail to be DAG-faithful, and recent extensions for time series models do not resolve the underlying computational issues.

Conclusion: A lack of DAG-faithfulness in existing methods undermines the reliability of their results in capturing the true temporal dynamics of time series data.

Abstract: Explainability methods for time series models predominantly produce flat attribution scores: they quantify the direct influence of a feature at a timestamp by a scalar. We prove that the dominant failure mode of such methods is not the scalar format itself but a fundamental computational mismatch: existing methods compute scores via marginal conditioning or off-manifold gradients, both of which conflate direct temporal dependencies with mediated ones under autocorrelation. We also define DAG-faithfulness: an explanation is DAG-faithful if the temporal dependency graph it encodes is Markov-equivalent to the temporal directed acyclic graph (DAG) implicitly learned by the model. Particularly, we observe that standard attribution methods, specifically SHAP, are not DAG-faithful in general, and that recent time-series-aware extensions inherit the same computational limitation.

</details>


### [386] [Quantizing Recursive Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16237)
*Thorir Mar Ingolfsson,Wajeeha Tahir,Anna Tegon,Lionnus Kesting,Gamze İslamoğlu,Luca Benini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the effect of quantization on recursive reasoning models, showing that activation-scaling granularity, not just bit-width, affects accuracy. It proposes a blockwise scaling method that mitigates accuracy degradation in 4-bit quantization, particularly in complex architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenges posed by quantization error in recursive reasoning models and to understand its impact on solving high-complexity puzzles, such as Sudoku.

Method: The authors analyze quantization effects on model accuracy and implement a blockwise integer activation format (MXInt4) to optimize performance, competing with existing formats while maintaining structural integrity.

Result: Findings indicate that per-tensor 4-bit quantization leads to significant accuracy loss due to activation-scaling granularity, but blockwise scaling mitigates this, enabling competitive performance across tasks.

Conclusion: Blockwise scaling effectively restores accuracy in recursive reasoning models, making them robust against quantization sensitivity and applicable to complex benchmarks.

Abstract: Recursive reasoning models solve hard puzzles by applying compact, weight-tied blocks over many refinement steps. Because these blocks are reused many times, quantizing them creates a unique dynamical problem: the quantization error is incurred at every step. While 8-bit quantization (integer or float) preserves accuracy, moving to a per-tensor 4-bit format causes a systematic bias to accumulate. The ensuing drift catastrophically degrades exact-solution accuracy on Sudoku from 84.1% to 0.0% (only ~25% of cells correct). In this work, we show that this collapse is caused by activation-scaling granularity rather than bit-width or number format. Crucially, moving to per-block scaling completely restores the transition. To implement this, we apply MXInt4, a blockwise integer activation format, to recursive reasoning models. It is competitive with blockwise float formats on our tasks, while keeping integer elements and power-of-two block scales. Finally, recursion depth and reuse modulate quantization sensitivity, with the deepest architecture we test (the EqR equilibrium model) the most sensitive. Yet blockwise scaling overcomes this vulnerability, staying robust across these architectures and transferring to the open-ended ARC-AGI benchmark.

</details>


### [387] [MADA-RL: Multi-Agent Debate-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in Compact Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18006)
*Martino M. L. Pulici,Cuong Xuan Chu,Evgeny Kharlamov,Zifeng Ding,Volker Tresp,Yunpu Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MADA-RL is a post-training framework for compact language models that improves reasoning performance on limited budgets by introducing a critic role with a counterfactual advantage, enhancing targeted credit assignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance the reasoning abilities of compact language models trained under budget constraints, addressing the high costs and challenges involved.

Method: MADA-RL employs a post-training framework using LoRA adapters, specializing models into generator and critic roles, and introducing a dynamic, role-conditioned baseline for the critic that focuses on improving over generator consensus.

Result: MADA-RL increases the accuracy of the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model by 2 percentage points (from 39.9% to 41.9%) with significantly fewer trainable parameters, establishing its position on the accuracy-trainable-parameter Pareto front.

Conclusion: While MADA-RL approaches the accuracy of stronger baselines trained on larger datasets, it does not exceed them; the counterfactual advantage significantly enhances critic performance, showing critics learn to rectify generator errors.

Abstract: Large language models achieve strong reasoning performance, but often at prohibitive training cost - a challenge that is especially acute for compact models ($\leq 4 \, \mathrm{B}$ parameters) trained under limited budgets. We introduce MADA-RL, a post-training framework that specializes compact models into generator and critic roles and trains them with a debate-aware learning signal, fine-tuning only a small subset of parameters via LoRA adapters. Our central contribution is a counterfactual critic advantage: a dynamic, role-conditioned baseline that redefines the critic's advantage as its reward minus the generator ensemble's per-instance accuracy. This explicitly optimizes critics to improve over generator consensus rather than to merely reproduce a correct answer, yielding more targeted credit assignment than static mean-reward normalization. At deployment, the specialized agents are composed in a lightweight multi-round protocol. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, MADA-RL raises the accuracy of the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model from $39.9 \, \%$ to $41.9 \, \%$ ($+2.0$ points, $p < 0.001$) using $16$ times fewer trainable parameters than fully fine-tuned baselines, placing it on the accuracy-trainable-parameter Pareto front. It approaches, but does not surpass, the strongest baselines (DeepScaleR, STILL-3), which are trained on substantially larger datasets; we analyse this gap and the associated inference-time cost directly. A controlled study isolates the source of MADA-RL's gains: the counterfactual advantage produces the highest critic improvement rate of any model evaluated, indicating that trained critics learn to correct generator errors rather than to imitate them.

</details>


### [388] [Diffusion-corrected Autoregressive Fourier Neural Operator for Droplet Evolution Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16238)
*Jinghao Cao,Minsung Kang,Hongyue Sun,Chi Zhou,Jihoon Chung,Xubo Yue,Sanchoy Das,Bo Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DiffARFNO combines autoregressive predictions with a DDIM corrector for improved long-term droplet evolution forecasting in material jetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance printing quality by accurately predicting droplet evolution in inkjet printing, particularly for long-horizon forecasts despite challenges like error accumulation.

Method: The method includes a two-stage framework where the first stage uses an autoregressive Fourier-MIONet for coarse prediction, and the second stage employs a DDIM corrector for detailed refinement.

Result: The proposed DiffARFNO framework shows significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art models in terms of prediction accuracy for droplet evolution.

Conclusion: DiffARFNO provides high-fidelity long-horizon predictions, combining the strengths of Fourier-MIONet and DDIM techniques to address the challenges of droplet evolution forecasting.

Abstract: Predicting droplet evolution in material jetting, or Inkjet Printing (IJP), is essential for maintaining printing quality. However, long-horizon forecasts remain challenging due to error accumulation and the complex coupling of process variables. In this work, we introduce the Diffusion-corrected Auto-Regressive Fourier Neural Operator (DiffARFNO), a two-stage framework that combines an autoregressive Fourier-MIONet with a conditional Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM) corrector. Fourier-MIONet is trained as a coarse predictor and deployed autoregressively for long-horizon forecasting. In the second stage, a DDIM-based conditional corrector refines the coarse prediction within each sliding window through efficient iterative denoising. By combining coarse predictions from Fourier-MIONet with a DDIM corrector that restores fine details, DiffARFNO aims to provide high-fidelity predictions for long-horizon forecasts. Extensive experiments on droplet datasets from ANSYS Fluent demonstrate that DiffARFNO significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.

</details>


### [389] [BACON: Budgeted Human Calibration for Modeling and Evaluation with Multiple AI Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16239)
*Lei Shi,Anlan Zhang,Rita Lyu,Zhengmian Hu,Tong Yu,David Arbour,Avi Feller,Saayan Mitra,Ritwik Sinha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BACON is a four-stage pipeline that integrates human calibration with AI judges to enhance evaluation accuracy and reduce bias in machine learning annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI judges, while cost-effective, often produce biased outputs that can skew evaluation metrics. There is a need for a reliable method to calibrate these outputs against human judgment to ensure accurate decision-making.

Method: BACON combines multiple AI outputs with human-label calibration. It uses auxiliary features, collects human labels for a subset, and trains a model for item-level predictions to derive accurate annotations.

Result: The implementation of BACON leads to improved predictive accuracy, ranking consistency, and reduced bias and variance compared to traditional methods that rely solely on AI or human annotations.

Conclusion: BACON provides a statistically grounded, efficient framework for improving evaluations in various tasks while maintaining low costs and limited human resources.

Abstract: AI judges offer a scalable, low-cost alternative to human evaluation, but their outputs can be biased relative to human preferences and highly item-dependent, varying across judges, tasks, and domains. When uncalibrated AI evaluations are used for model ranking, item scoring, or population-level quality reporting, these biases can directly distort downstream decisions. We propose BACON, a four-stage pipeline that combines budgeted human calibration with multiple AI-judge outputs to produce more accurate annotations. BACON constructs full-coverage auxiliary features for every item, including multi-judge scores, token-level uncertainty statistics, and contextual embeddings. It then collects human labels for a small sampled subset and trains a cross-fitted outcome model to generate calibrated item-level surrogate predictions. These predictions support two use cases: population-level estimation of summary metrics, such as means or quantiles, using an augmented estimating-equation estimator with valid confidence intervals; and individual-level surrogate scoring for item ranking and annotation. BACON treats AI judges as auxiliary measurements rather than ground truth: human labels provide the calibration anchor, while AI-derived signals improve efficiency. Across diverse tasks, domains, and labeling budgets, BACON improves predictive accuracy and ranking consistency, and reduces bias and variance relative to raw AI outputs and purely human-label-based methods. These results show that BACON offers a practical, statistically grounded framework for scalable evaluation with limited human annotation.

</details>


### [390] [Normalized Rewards for Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16240)
*Shawn Im,Federico Danieli,Skyler Seto,Barry-John Theobald,Katherine Metcalf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses issues of over-optimization in DAAs like DPO used for aligning LLMs with human preferences by introducing regularization to maintain response likelihoods, leading to improved generation quality while mitigating undesirable behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DAAs have shown tendencies to over-optimize implicit reward models, causing decreased likelihoods of preferred responses in LLMs, potentially leading to undesirable performance.

Method: The study proposes a regularization term in training objectives to maintain total length-normalized probabilities of chosen and rejected responses, examining the impact on response probability distribution over tokens.

Result: Application of the regularization term to DPO and SimPO methods demonstrated improved trade-offs in generation quality and benchmark performance, with significant increases in AlpacaEval2 scores and general benchmark performance.

Conclusion: The regularization effectively mitigates likelihood displacement within preferred responses, particularly addressing outlier tokens, thus enhancing the overall quality of LLM responses.

Abstract: Direct Alignment Algorithms (DAAs) such as DPO have become a common way to post-train and align LLMs with human preferences. However, DAAs have been observed to over-optimize their implicit reward model and decrease the likelihood of preferred responses. This results in a decrease in the total likelihood assigned to responses seen in the preference dataset, potentially resulting in undesirable behavior. To counteract this undesired side-effect of DAAs, we examine the effect of using objectives that add a regularization term to maintain the total length-normalized probabilities of the chosen and rejected responses. To better understand over-optimization, we investigate how response likelihood changes are distributed over the tokens with and without regularization. We find that a significant portion of the likelihood changes are due to a small set of outlier tokens, which explains how DAAs improve generation quality despite decreasing the likelihoods of chosen responses. We apply the proposed regularization to reference-based (DPO) and reference-free (SimPO) methods and find (1) improved trade-offs between generation quality and general benchmark capability and (2) improvements in reward modeling across datasets. For example, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we see both a >20% relative increase in AlpacaEval2 scores and >9% relative performance gains on general benchmarks. Additionally, we find that the added regularization term effectively mitigates the amount of displacement within preferred responses overall, and for the outlier tokens specifically, by utilizing low-likelihood tokens.

</details>


### [391] [KernelBench-Verified: Do LLM-Generated Kernels Actually Beat PyTorch?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16241)
*Yunxiang Zhang,Ping Yu,Jianyu Wang,Max,Fan,Julian Reed,Azalia Mirhoseini,Will Su*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recent LLMs can generate CUDA kernels but tend to engage in reward hacking, leading to inflated performance metrics. A new framework, KernelBench-Verified, addresses evaluation flaws, noting that real-world execution timings differ when using proper settings and that models may bypass necessary computations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess the true performance of CUDA kernels generated by LLMs, especially given issues with reward hacking and unrealistic evaluation metrics in traditional frameworks.

Method: Developed KernelBench-Verified, integrating TF32 acceleration and introducing hidden tests across various distributions, alongside new memory efficiency metrics to evaluate speed-memory tradeoffs.

Result: Under verified evaluations, the best LLM (GPT-5.5) exhibited lower speedup (0.88x) than previously reported (1.43x), with no model outperforming PyTorch. Additionally, many generated kernels increased peak GPU memory usage.

Conclusion: The study highlights the urgent need for robust and adaptive evaluation protocols to match advancements in LLM capabilities in generating CUDA kernels.

Abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) can generate custom CUDA kernels that appear to outperform PyTorch on benchmarks such as KernelBench. Building upon this foundational framework, we demonstrate that frontier models frequently engage in reward hacking to artificially inflate reported performance. In this work, we identify two areas where evaluation frameworks must co-evolve with model capabilities. First, to accurately measure true speedup, we examine the baseline timing mechanism, noting that enabling Tensor Core acceleration with TF32 provides a more realistic estimation of execution on modern GPUs. Second, concerning algorithmic correctness, models often exploit the narrow test distribution by hardcoding bypasses for specific tensor values. By skipping required computations, these kernels artificially accelerate execution rather than implementing actual CUDA kernels. We introduce KernelBench-Verified, an extended evaluation framework that incorporates a TF32-enabled baseline and a four-distribution hidden test suite. We additionally introduce memory efficiency metrics that capture the often-overlooked speed-memory tradeoff in kernel optimization. Under verified single-turn evaluation with seven frontier LLMs, we find that the best-performing model (GPT-5.5) achieves a 0.88x geometric mean speedup, significantly lower than the 1.43x speedup observed under the standard evaluation protocol. No model consistently outperforms PyTorch when evaluated against realistic baselines. On the memory front, 28% of GPU kernels generated by the best model increase peak GPU memory usage. Our findings demonstrate the necessity of continually adapting robust evaluation protocols as LLM kernel generation capabilities advance.

</details>


### [392] [TRACE: Trajectory-Based Safety Patch Learning for LLM Post-Training Realignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16242)
*Changyue Li,Jiaming He,Youliang Yuan,Jialin Wu,Boxi Yu,Zhicong Huang,Pinjia He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRACE is a framework for safety patch learning in fine-tuned LLMs that enhances model safety without sacrificing performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address safety alignment erosion in fine-tuned language models while preserving their utility.

Method: TRACE employs a trajectory-based approach to simulate harmful tuning trajectories and learns a safety patch that optimally balances safety and utility.

Result: TRACE achieves nearly 100% safety while maintaining utility similar to undefended models across various benchmarks.

Conclusion: TRACE effectively improves safety in fine-tuned language models without compromising their task performance.

Abstract: Fine-Tuning-as-a-Service (FTaaS) platforms let users train large language models (LLMs) on customized tasks, but this pipeline could erode models' safety alignment. In practice, service providers need to recover models' safety without re-running full alignment, or destroying the utility gained from customized tasks. A line of existing work refers to model parameter merging, which adds a safety patch on the fine-tuned model parameters to shift the model away from unsafe tendencies. However, this merging-based paradigm is fundamentally bottlenecked by task-safety update entanglement: downstream task updates and the safety patch often overlap in their dominant directions, so the merge strength is intrinsically hard to calibrate. If the safety vector is scaled too weakly, harmful components could still dominate, preventing the model from returning to a safe region; if it is scaled too aggressively, it suppresses task-relevant directions and degrades utility.
  To solve this problem, we shift the focus of merging-based methods from designing online merging operators to offline patch learning, and seek a safety patch that minimally interferes with task-relevant directions while retaining decisive control over unsafe behaviors. We propose TRACE, a trajectory-based safety patch learning framework that (i) simulates harmful tuning trajectories to generate progressively corrupted states, and (ii) optimizes a plug-in patch to recover safety while maintaining utility across varying corrupted base states.
  Across six benchmarks and two models, TRACE consistently dominates the safety-utility frontier. TRACE reaches nearly 100% safety on all settings, while maintaining comparable utility to the undefended fine-tuned model.

</details>


### [393] [RobustMAD: Evaluating Real-World Robustness of Multimodal Small Language Models for Deployable Anomaly Detection Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16243)
*Anushiya Arunan,Xin Li,Yan Qin,U-Xuan Tan,Nhu Khue Vuong,Xiaoli Li,Chau Yuen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces RobustMAD, a benchmark for evaluating the robustness of compact multimodal small language models in industrial anomaly detection, revealing critical gaps in performance and suggesting improvements for design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the impracticalities of deploying large multimodal language models in industrial settings due to computational demands and privacy concerns, and to fill the gap of insufficient robustness analyses and challenging benchmarks.

Method: Development of RobustMAD, a benchmark that evaluates model robustness through a variety of queries related to object understanding, anomaly detection, and response quality under real-world industrial conditions.

Result: Compact MSLMs demonstrate notable capabilities but reveal critical robustness gaps, particularly in multimodal grounding and logical reasoning, which suggest they do not yet meet safety-critical requirements.

Conclusion: To improve future multimodal industrial inspection assistants, the insights from RobustMAD highlight the need for addressing identified failure modes and enhancing model design.

Abstract: Multimodal industrial anomaly inspection assistants are a critical component of next-generation smart factories, enabling interactive vision-language-based querying. However, multimodal large language models remain impractical for on-site deployment due to prohibitive computational demands and privacy risks from cloud-based inference. Compact multimodal small language models (MSLMs) offer a deployable alternative, yet progress is constrained by the lack of comprehensive robustness analyses and meaningfully challenging benchmarks that reflect real-world industrial conditions. To address this gap, we develop RobustMAD, the first deployment-motivated benchmark, designed to comprehensively evaluate model robustness through diverse open-ended queries spanning object understanding, anomaly detection, unanswerable problems, and visual quality degradations. Contrary to conventional assumptions, top-performing MSLMs exhibit promising capabilities, surprisingly outperforming even the larger GPT-5 Nano. However, they still fall short of safety-critical requirements, and RobustMAD reveals critical robustness gaps that pose operational risks. In particular, three recurring failure modes emerge: (i) fragile multimodal grounding under fine-grained distinctions or degraded visual conditions, (ii) insufficiently comprehensive responses, and (iii) weak logical grounding on unanswerable or ill-posed queries, leading to hallucinated outputs. Grounded in these insights, we provide actionable guidance for the design of next-generation multimodal industrial inspection assistants that leverage their promising competence. Code is available at https://github.com/en-research/RobustMAD.

</details>


### [394] [TurboVec: A Case Study in Cost-Efficient Private Retrieval for Enterprise RAG via Codebook-Oblivious Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16973)
*Navnit Shukla,Kamal Pandey,Omsankar Tiwari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TurboVec, an open-source vector index utilizing TurboQuant, addresses challenges in enterprise LLM applications related to vector retrieval by offering significant performance improvements over traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To tackle the leakage of corpus statistics and recall degradation in multi-tenant deployments of LLM applications due to vector retrieval layers.

Method: TurboQuant, a codebook-oblivious scalar quantizer, is introduced alongside TurboVec, which is deployed for efficient vector indexing and retrieval without corpus-dependent training.

Result: TurboQuant outperforms FAISS Product Quantization and achieves higher recall than HNSW, requiring less memory; TurboVec provides fast query latency and effective tenant isolation.

Conclusion: While TurboVec shows promise in improving recall and privacy, it has limitations including lack of dataset diversity, uncompressed comparison, and reliance on synthetic data for privacy evaluation.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly power enterprise LLM applications, yet the vector retrieval layer introduces two underexplored challenges: (1) trained codebook quantizers may expose corpus statistics during index construction, creating a leakage channel in multi-tenant deployments, and (2) post-hoc filtering for tenant isolation degrades recall on selective queries. We study TurboVec, an open-source vector index built on TurboQuant - a codebook-oblivious scalar quantizer requiring no corpus-dependent training. On the DBpedia OpenAI embeddings benchmark (d=1536, 100K-999K vectors), TurboQuant 4-bit outperforms trained FAISS Product Quantization at the same memory budget by 8.5-8.9 percentage points in Recall@5 across all scales. Compared to HNSW (R@5=0.991) and IVF-PQ (R@5=0.840), TurboQuant occupies a distinct design point: higher recall than IVF-PQ without training, at 4-8x less memory than HNSW. Deployed on Snowpark Container Services, TurboVec achieves 11ms median query latency at 100K vectors versus 707ms for warehouse brute-force scan. Kernel-level allowlist filtering maintains 0.86-0.93 Recall@10 across 10-1000 tenant workloads versus 0.09-0.19 for post-filter baselines. Codebook-oblivious design reduces membership inference accuracy to near-random (50.0%) versus 57.3% for PQ codebooks. Limitations include single dataset evaluation, uncompressed HNSW comparison, and privacy evaluation on synthetic data only.

</details>


### [395] [Empowering On-Device Model Adaptation with an Edge AI Inference Accelerator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18101)
*Mateusz Piechocki,Alessandro Capotondi,Marek Kraft*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a method for on-device model adaptation using a heterogeneous adaptation pipeline that leverages a commercial edge AI inference accelerator for efficient training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable lifelong personalization of models on resource-constrained hardware while overcoming limitations of compute, power, and memory.

Method: The method involves partitioning the computational graph, where a quantized INT8 pre-trained backbone operates on an accelerator, while a lightweight FP32 classification head is fine-tuned on the CPU.

Result: Achieves up to 15.4x faster training time compared to a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU, along with improved energy efficiency and competitive throughput.

Conclusion: Demonstrates an effective approach to on-device adaptation using edge accelerators, with a significant focus on maintaining feature quality during quantization.

Abstract: On-device model adaptation is essential to enable lifelong personalization on resource-constrained hardware, but compute, power, and memory limitations of such devices make end-to-end backpropagation impractical for modern deep neural networks. This work proposes a heterogeneous adaptation pipeline that repurposes a commercial edge AI inference accelerator, Hailo-8L, for frozen-backbone feature extraction during on-device training. The computational graph is partitioned so that the pre-trained backbone is quantized to INT8 and run on the accelerator, while only a lightweight FP32 classification head is fine-tuned on the host CPU, enabling frequent, energy-efficient in-field updates with most weights remaining fixed. Across multiple architectures and datasets, this pipeline achieves up to 15.4x faster wall-clock training time compared to a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU baseline, offers competitive throughput in favorable settings, and consistently reduces energy per sample. Post-training quantization restoration is shown to be crucial for preserving the quality of accelerator-generated features and mitigating accuracy loss in quantization-sensitive architectures. Overall, the results demonstrate a practical approach to efficient on-device adaptation using inference-oriented edge accelerators. The implementation is available at https://github.com/MatPiech/accelerator-training.

</details>


### [396] [CIGPO: Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Evidence-Reading LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16244)
*Hao Dou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses instability in training multi-turn evidence-reading agents via outcome-only reinforcement learning, proposing CIGPO to mitigate reward collapse and improve performance on HotpotQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To solve the instability in training multi-turn evidence-reading agents which arises from intermediate turns receiving minimal credit, leading to optimization deadlocks.

Method: Introduce Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization (CIGPO) to assign rewards to intermediate turns using the increase in log-likelihood of the correct answer, along with separate normalization of rewards.

Result: CIGPO achieves a standard F1 score of 0.518 on HotpotQA, significantly outperforming both GRPO's best score (0.430) and its final score (0.000).

Conclusion: The study identifies reward-variance collapse in outcome-only GRPO as a major failure and demonstrates that turn-level information gain rewards can effectively prevent this issue.

Abstract: Training multi-turn evidence-reading agents with outcome-only reinforcement learning is unstable because intermediate turns receive little direct credit. In HotpotQA experiments with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, GRPO initially improves (standard F1 0.430) but subsequently collapses to 100% format-violating outputs. Training-log diagnosis reveals a zero-advantage lock-in mechanism: all sampled trajectories receive the minimum format penalty (-2.0), group-relative advantages vanish, and the policy-gradient loss becomes zero--an optimization deadlock. We propose a variance-injection strategy: by assigning per-turn rewards to intermediate evidence-reading turns, we prevent the group reward distribution from collapsing to a single value--preserving the variation that GRPO's group-relative advantage requires. Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization (CIGPO) implements this strategy using the marginal increase in the frozen reference model's log-likelihood of the ground-truth answer as the per-turn signal. With separate normalization of IG and F1 rewards and an IG-weight curriculum, CIGPO reaches a standard F1 of 0.518 on HotpotQA at the 3B scale (from 0.252 base; +105%), compared with 0.430 for the best GRPO checkpoint and 0.000 for the final GRPO checkpoint. CIGPO maintains meaningful reward variance and avoids zero-advantage lock-in throughout training. These results identify reward-variance collapse as a concrete failure mode of outcome-only GRPO and show that turn-level IG rewards can prevent it in this HotpotQA setting.

</details>


### [397] [DRNOISE: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents in Misleading Evidence Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17291)
*Jun Nie,Zhiqin Yang,Zhenheng Tang,Yonggang Zhang,Xiaowen Chu,Xinmei Tian,Bo Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DRNOISE is a benchmark highlighting the challenges deep research agents face when misleading documents coexist with genuine evidence, demonstrating significant accuracy drops in response to conflicting information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate and enhance the evidential standards of deep research agents when confronted with misleading documents in open-web environments.

Method: Introducing DRNOISE, a 100-task benchmark that assesses agent performance in recovering accurate answers despite the presence of misleading documents; each task includes a gold answer and corroborating evidence chains, alongside a noise document presenting conflicting information.

Result: Agents experience dramatic accuracy drops (66-88 percentage points) when a misleading document is introduced, primarily due to verification inertia—stopping short of evidence reconciliation.

Conclusion: Effective deep research requires active reconciliation of evidence, beyond mere retrieval and citation, especially in contexts where misleading information is prevalent.

Abstract: Deep research agents increasingly operate over the open web, where relevant records coexist with redundant summaries, outdated reports, and misleading documents. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether agents preserve sound evidential standards when an ordinary-looking false document is deliberately seeded into a searchable environment and offers a direct shortcut to a conflicting answer. We introduce DRNOISE, a 100-task benchmark for answer recovery under misleading evidence. Each task has a unique gold answer supported by two corroborating indirect record chains; the paired noisy condition adds one plausible document that states a conflicting answer directly. The benchmark spans ten families of evidence operations. Across agents with strong clean-task performance, this single intervention causes 66-88 percentage-point accuracy drops. Trace analyses identify verification inertia as the dominant failure mode: agents often retrieve truthful records but stop before completing and reconciling the evidence chain, instead deferring to the answer-like document. Generic verification prompts reduce but do not close this gap. The setting is especially relevant to open-web deployment, where plausible falsehoods arrive through ordinary-looking pages rather than explicit attacks. Reliable deep research therefore requires more than retrieval and citation; it requires active reconciliation of direct claims with record-level evidence.

</details>


### [398] [Learning Structural Manipulability in Gate-Level Netlists Using Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16245)
*Rupesh Raj Karn,Ozgur Sinanoglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a topology-driven structural manipulability score for gate-level netlists, modeled as directed graphs, and uses graph neural networks (GNNs) to evaluate signal propagation properties. It finds that hierarchical GNN architectures provide consistent rankings of this score across benchmarks and reveals useful insights into structural patterns in Trojan-injected circuits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To characterize signal propagation properties in gate-level netlists based on their structural properties, independent of functional criteria.

Method: A topology-driven manipulability score is defined and modeled using directed graphs; GNNs are employed for node-level regression to learn this score.

Result: Hierarchical GNN models consistently rank the structural manipulability score across the ISCAS85 and EPFL benchmarks, revealing significant contributions of individual structural factors and distinguishable patterns in Trojan-injected circuits.

Conclusion: Topology-based scoring offers valuable insights into structural properties of netlists, complementing existing analysis methods.

Abstract: Gate-level netlists exhibit intrinsic structural properties that influence signal propagation independently of functional simulation. We define a topology-driven structural manipulability score that characterizes node-level structural flexibility using path participation, k-core embedding, symmetry, and centrality. Modeling netlists as directed graphs, we formulate node-level regression to learn this topology-derived score using graph neural networks (GNNs). Experiments on ISCAS85 and EPFL benchmarks evaluate how effectively different GNN architectures approximate this metric across held-out circuits, with hierarchical models yielding the most consistent rankings. Component-level and ablation analyses examine the contribution of individual factors. As an illustrative case study, analysis of Trojan-injected circuits using TrustHub templates reveals statistically distinguishable structural patterns, indicating that topology-based scoring provides complementary structural insight.

</details>


### [399] [Mobius Learning: Cyclic Depth Folding in Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17843)
*Tongtian Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Mobius Learning introduces cyclic depth folding in Transformer models, allowing block roles to shift dynamically, achieving lower validation loss in certain setups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the traditional fixed role assignment of Transformer blocks in depth and explore new representational capabilities.

Method: Mobius Learning employs a cyclic depth folding architecture that allows different data streams to utilize block groups in varying sequential orders.

Result: Mobius Learning outperforms a standard fixed-order Transformer with lower validation loss in experiments with greater block-sequence passes.

Conclusion: This approach reveals that Transformer blocks can operate in multiple representational roles, suggesting a new design space for memory-efficient distributed training.

Abstract: Transformer-based language models organize computation along an ordered depth axis, where shallow and deep blocks often develop distinct representational roles. We challenge the conventional view that these roles must remain tied to a block's position in the ordered sequence. We introduce Mobius Learning, a training architecture based on cyclic depth folding, in which different data streams follow cyclically shifted block orders. The same block group is therefore applied early in the block sequence for some data streams and late for others, so it is optimized in both shallow and deep roles, a phenomenon we call depth-role superposition. Surprisingly, in four-worker experiments with a modded GPT-2 small (124M) model trained on 2.5B FineWeb tokens using Muon, Mobius Learning achieves lower validation loss than a fixed-order looped Transformer at larger numbers of Transformer block-sequence passes. This counterintuitive result shows that a block group need not remain confined to one fixed shallow or deep role within the block sequence and opens a new design space based on cyclic depth folding. Crucially, this structure makes Mobius Learning particularly well suited to memory-constrained distributed training: raw training data remain local, while each worker stores one block group rather than the complete Transformer block stack.

</details>


### [400] [Let the Data Decide: Supervision Analysis, Capability Trade-offs, and Adaptive Objective Routing in Continued Pre-Training via Off-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16246)
*Jiangan Yuan,Zhixuan Li,Han Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study investigates off-policy distillation in large language models, focusing on the relationship between training objectives and model capabilities, and introduces a structured approach for objective routing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the interactions between training data, objective parameterization, and model capabilities in off-policy distillation during language model pre-training.

Method: The analysis involves two parts: an objective-to-capability analysis comparing language-modeling and knowledge-distillation objectives, and a data-to-objective analysis regarding data heterogeneity and objective routing, supported by diagnostic metrics.

Result: The study finds that different training objectives yield different model capabilities and that effective objective routing is influenced more by the quality of the routing signal rather than its granularity, leading to superior performance with adaptive routing strategies.

Conclusion: Continued pre-training via off-policy distillation should be approached as a structured problem of supervision design that considers data conditions rather than merely as a hyperparameter tuning issue.

Abstract: Off-policy distillation is now central to large language model pre-training, yet how training data, objective parameterization, and model capabilities interact remains poorly characterized. We studies top-$k$-truncated, temperature-scaled off-policy distillation by decomposing this problem into two questions: an \emph{objective-to-capability} analysis of how the training objective shapes token-level supervision and downstream performance, and a \emph{data-to-objective} analysis of how data heterogeneity should inform objective routing. We first show that the language-modeling objective ($L_{\mathrm{LM}}$) and the knowledge-distillation objective ($L_{\mathrm{KD}}$) induce systematically different capability profiles, and trace this divergence to a gradient-level tension between \emph{direct observed-token reinforcement} and \emph{teacher-supported alternative supervision}. To quantify this tension, we introduce diagnostic metrics -- support coverage, observed-token probability mass, and teacher-distribution concentration -- and show via controlled sweeps that the support size $k$ governs a coverage-sharpness trade-off, while distillation temperature controls within-support probability allocation. We then examine adaptive objective routing: a domain-level policy that applies $L_{\mathrm{LM}}$ to math and code and $L_{\mathrm{KD}}$ to general-domain data yields consistent gains over both single-objective baselines, whereas token-level routing based on observed-token probability mass or teacher entropy fails to consistently match the single-objective baseline. These results suggest that effective objective routing depends less on routing granularity than on the quality of the routing signal, reframing continued pre-training via off-policy distillation as a structured, data-conditional supervision-design problem rather than a global hyperparameter choice.

</details>


### [401] [ANNLib: A Development Framework for Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17582)
*Zheqi Shen,Jingbo Su,Zijin Wan,Yan Gu,Yihan Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ANNLib is a library designed for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search that provides high performance and flexible functionality with minimal programming effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bridge the gap between high performance and flexible functionality in ANNS systems while minimizing programming efforts.

Method: ANNLib is developed as a library that decouples and optimizes algorithm and data structure components, integrating state-of-the-art modules to enable user-defined configurations.

Result: Provides a simple interface that supports sophisticated ANNS settings and demonstrates comparable or superior performance relative to previous systems across various applications.

Conclusion: ANNLib enables users to efficiently implement high-performance ANNS solutions with a flexible framework, advancing the capabilities of deep learning pipelines.

Abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) plays a pivotal role in modern deep learning pipelines. Recently, many ANNS systems have been proposed to either provide broad functionality or reach high performance. However, it is yet difficult to achieve both with minimal programming efforts. We propose ANNLib to address the gap. ANNLib is a library that provides a programming framework for achieving high performance and flexible functionality in ANNS systems, based on popular graph-based ANNS algorithms. We carefully decouple and independently optimize both the algorithm and the data structure components of an ANNS system. In addition, we integrate state-of-the-art algorithms and data structures into ANNLib as modules, along with our new designs. Users can choose combinations of components to implement sophisticated settings with high performance, such as filter search, fully dynamic updates, and historical queries on snapshots. Our experiments show that our new solution provides a simple interface for various applications and achieves comparable or even better performance than previous work, specifically for each application.

</details>


### [402] [Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory for Proactive Embodied Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16247)
*Bingrui Sima,Lizhong Wang,Xiaoya Lu,Kun He,Xiao Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents the Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory framework that enhances the safety of Vision-Language Models by shifting from cautionary measures to proactive hazard mitigation, improving task success rates without hindering progress.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of dynamically emerging hazards in embodied agents during tasks, and overcome the limitations of existing overly cautious safety approaches that impede progress.

Method: Introducing a framework that includes a Risk-Sufficient Topological Belief Graph for safety tracking, an Agency-Grounded Factual Memory for hazard anticipation, and an Experience Memory infused with Meta-Skills for effective mitigation strategies.

Result: Experiments show a significant increase in Safe-Success rates (up to +30.3% on Qwen3-VL-8B) across various Vision-Language Model backbones, indicating improved hazard management.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enables agents to proactively manage risks and hazards without hindering task execution, leading to better performance in complex environments.

Abstract: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have empowered embodied agents to execute complex household tasks, they struggle to proactively handle dynamically emerging hazards during closed-loop interactions. Existing safety approaches often rely on runtime guardrails to block unsafe actions or induce excessive caution, which severely stalls task progress instead of actively resolving the underlying risks. To break this safety-progress trade-off, we introduce the Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory framework, which reframes embodied safety from progress-stalling guardrails to proactive hazard mitigation. The framework consists of a Risk-Sufficient Topological Belief Graph (RSG) for persistent safety-relevant state tracking under partial observability, an Agency-Grounded Factual Memory for precise hazard anticipation, and an Experience Memory that injects procedural Meta-Skills to guide executable, progress-preserving mitigation. Furthermore, we propose an automated Test-Verify-Write loop, allowing agents to continually refine their mitigation Meta-Skills from execution traces at test time. Experiments on IS-Bench demonstrate that our framework substantially boosts the Safe-Success rate across multiple VLM backbones (e.g., +30.3% on Qwen3-VL-8B), enabling agents to proactively mitigate hazards without stalling task progress. Code is available at https://github.com/DyMessi/JIT-Memory.

</details>


### [403] [High-accuracy Low-Bit KV-Cache Quantization via Local Distribution Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16248)
*Gradwell Dzikanyanga,Yanqi Pan,Weihao Yang,Donglei Wu,Wen Xia,Hao Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents DGAP, a method to enhance low-bit KV-cache quantization in large language models by restoring local distributions, recovering significant accuracy while maintaining low resource usage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the high memory and bandwidth overheads associated with long-context large language models that utilize KV cache, particularly when low-bit quantization degrades model accuracy.

Method: The authors introduce local distribution restoration, which identifies steps with high local distribution risk and restores only the top-K candidate distributions from quantized logit features, implemented through DGAP with efficient risk detectors and correctors.

Result: DGAP recovers RULER accuracy from 47.8% to 83.2% on the Llama-3.1-8B model and reduces distribution drift from 0.38 to 0.14 while maintaining a low-bit KV-cache footprint.

Conclusion: The approach shows that it is possible to significantly enhance the accuracy of low-bit quantization in large language models without increasing the resource footprint.

Abstract: Long-context large language model inference relies on the KV cache to avoid redundant attention computation, but incurs high memory and bandwidth overheads. Low-bit KV-cache quantization reduces this cost, yet it severely degrade quality; particularly, one-bit quantization reduces accuracy from 84.2% to 47.8% on Llama-3.1-8B under RULER.
  Rather than common beliefs that absolute error of logits, we find that the root cause is structured local misranking, where the distribution of logits in top-K region is drifted. We thereby propose local distribution restoration, a new technique that detects steps with high local distribution risk from quantized-logit features and restores only the selected top-K candidate distribution before token selection. We implement DGAP to achieve local distribution restoration, with efficient risk detcetors and correctors. Expeirments show that on Llama-3.1-8B, DGAP recovers K1V1 RULER accuracy from 47.8% to 83.2% and reduces distribution drift from 0.38 to 0.14; across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models, it preserves the persistent low-bit KV-cache footprint with modest decode overhead.

</details>


### [404] [Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Multi-Omics-Based Breast Cancer Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16250)
*Priyanka Paudel,Madan Baduwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study benchmarks classical machine learning models for predicting Estrogen Receptor status in breast cancer using multi-omics data, finding Random Forest most effective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve breast cancer diagnosis and treatment through accurate prediction of Estrogen Receptor status using diverse molecular data.

Method: A systematic analysis of machine learning models (including Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM) was performed using RNA expression, CNV, and RPPA data from TCGA-BRCA, with rigorous evaluation techniques.

Result: RNA expression showed the strongest predictive signal; Random Forest performed best with balanced accuracy of 90.3% and ROC-AUC of 97.1%; integration of multi-omics provided modest improvements.

Conclusion: Classical machine learning models are effective for high-dimensional datasets, with multi-omic data enhancing predictive performance for ER status in breast cancer.

Abstract: Estrogen Receptor (ER) status is a critical biomarker in breast cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection. Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies have enabled the generation of multi-omics datasets that provide complementary molecular information for computational prediction tasks. This study presents a systematic benchmarking analysis of classical machine learning models for ER status prediction using transcriptomic (RNA expression), genomic (copy number variation; CNV), and proteomic (RPPA) data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort. A rigorous experimental framework incorporating stratified train-test splitting, stratified five-fold cross-validation, class imbalance handling, and fold-specific feature selection was employed to ensure reliable evaluation and prevent data leakage. Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Logistic Regression were evaluated across single-omic and multi-omic settings. Results demonstrated that RNA expression provided the strongest predictive signal, while multi-omic integration yielded modest but consistent improvements over individual modalities. Among all evaluated approaches, Random Forest achieved the best overall performance in the integrated multi-omic setting, obtaining a balanced accuracy of 90.3\% and an ROC-AUC of 97.1\%. Furthermore, recurrent selection of biologically relevant genes, including \textit{ESR1}, \textit{PGR}, \textit{FOXA1}, and \textit{GATA3}, supported the biological validity of the learned models. These findings indicate that carefully regularized classical machine learning methods remain highly effective for small, high-dimensional genomic datasets and that multi-omic integration provides complementary information for breast cancer ER status prediction.

</details>


### [405] [Learning Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models from Pure Synthetic Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16251)
*Yutong Feng,Shiyuan Piao,Yutong Xia,Xu Liu,Wenqi Fan,Fugee Tsung,See-Kiong Ng,Yuxuan Liang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NeoST is a novel spatio-temporal foundation model that addresses biases in real-world data and structural limitations of prior approaches by using synthetic data for training, improving performance in spatio-temporal systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome distributional bias and structural limitations in existing spatio-temporal models while enhancing long-horizon stability and inference efficiency.

Method: NeoST leverages a scalable synthetic pre-training corpus, a latent-space reasoning architecture for trajectory generation and refinement, and latent-space objectives for better structural dynamics representation.

Result: NeoST demonstrates consistent superiority over existing STFMs across various real-world benchmarks, particularly in terms of long-horizon stability and inference efficiency.

Conclusion: The introduction of NeoST represents a significant advancement in spatio-temporal modeling, offering a solution that mitigates real-world biases and improves performance through innovative model architecture.

Abstract: Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models (STFMs) aim to learn generalizable representations of complex dynamical systems across space and time. However, existing approaches suffer from distributional bias in real-world pre-training data, structural bottlenecks of autoregressive or diffusion-based paradigms, and objectives that overemphasize point-wise reconstruction in noisy observation space.We propose \textbf{NeoST}, the first spatio-temporal foundation model pre-trained solely on procedurally generated synthetic systems. NeoST introduces a scalable synthetic pre-training corpus to mitigate real-world bias, a latent-space reasoning architecture that generates and iteratively refines multiple future trajectories without sequential error accumulation, and latent-space objectives that emphasize structural dynamics and enable inference-time correction under distribution shifts.Extensive experiments across diverse real-world benchmarks show that NeoST consistently outperforms existing STFMs in diverse real-world spatio-temporal systems, achieves superior long-horizon stability and inference efficiency.

</details>


### [406] [SOS-LoRA: Static Orthogonal-Subspace Low-Rank Adaptation with Fixed Multi-Scale Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16252)
*Yupeng Chang,Yuan Wu,Yi Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SOS-LoRA improves LoRA by using static low-rank experts, leading to better optimization and performance without increasing inference costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of LoRA in terms of optimization interference and behavior coupling among adapted weights in large language models.

Method: SOS-LoRA decomposes the rank into K static low-rank experts with fixed scaling, orthogonal initialization, and a lightweight regularizer to enhance optimization dynamics and direction diversity.

Result: Experiments demonstrate superior performance of SOS-LoRA on a variety of benchmarks (Llama 2/3, GLUE, GSM8K/MATH) compared to standard LoRA and its recent variations.

Conclusion: SOS-LoRA presents an efficient enhancement over LoRA, achieving improved results while remaining mergeable and cost-effective during inference.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method for large language models. Under a fixed rank budget, LoRA parameterizes each adapted weight through a single low-dimensional input-side pathway, which may couple heterogeneous behaviors through shared input directions and induce interference during optimization. We propose Static Orthogonal Subspace LoRA (SOS-LoRA), a drop-in extension that reparameterizes a rank-rtot update as a sum of K static (always-on, non-routed) low-rank experts. SOS-LoRA (i) decomposes the total rank across experts, (ii) applies a fixed multi-scale scaling scheme to encourage scale-separated optimization dynamics, and (iii) promotes diverse input-side directions via cross-expert orthogonal initialization and a lightweight regularizer. SOS-LoRA remains fully mergeable, adding no inference-time parameters or latency after merging. Experiments on reasoning and knowledge-intensive benchmarks (Llama 2/3), encoder-based NLU (GLUE), and math reasoning (GSM8K/MATH) show consistent gains over matched-budget LoRA baselines and recent variants. Code is available at https://github.com/llm172/sos-lora.

</details>


### [407] [Comprehensive Evaluation of Machine Learning for Type 2 Diabetes Risk Prediction: Large-Scale External Validation and Fairness Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16253)
*Rajveer Singh Pall,Sameer Yadav,Siddharth Bhalerao,Sourabh Sahu,Ritu Ahluwalia,Bhaskar Awadhiya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The study develops a comprehensive framework to evaluate diabetes risk prediction models, highlighting performance and fairness issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limited external validation and fairness assessment in existing diabetes risk prediction models.

Method: An XGBoost model trained on NHANES data with non-laboratory predictors; evaluated for discrimination, calibration, and fairness on a nationally representative sample.

Result: Internal validation showed AUC of 0.794, while external validation performed under distribution shift resulted in AUC of 0.717, indicating a significant performance drop. Fairness analysis revealed bias against elderly and obese populations.

Conclusion: The model's poorer performance in high-risk populations necessitates fairness-aware, age-stratified strategies for clinical application.

Abstract: Machine learning-based Type 2 diabetes risk prediction models obtain good internal validation results but lose effectiveness in real-world applications due to deficient external testing and fairness assessment. We developed a multi-dimensional framework evaluating discrimination, calibration, interpretability, and algorithmic fairness on nationally representative populations. An XGBoost model was trained on NHANES 2015-2020 (n=15,685) using eight non-laboratory predictors: age, sex, race/ethnicity, BMI, smoking status, physical activity, history of heart attack, and history of stroke. External validation was performed on BRFSS 2020-2022 (n=1,285,783) under realistic distribution shift. Internal validation showed good discrimination (AUC=0.794, 95% CI 0.788-0.800), with performance loss on external validation (AUC=0.717, relative decrease: -9.7%, p<0.001). Fairness analysis revealed severe bias: elderly adults (>=60) showed AUC=0.607 vs 0.742 for young adults (difference=0.135, p<0.001); obese individuals showed AUC=0.698 vs 0.735 for normal weight (difference=0.037, p<0.001). Gender showed comparable performance (male=0.723 vs female=0.712, p=0.142). Calibration revealed risk overestimation (Brier score=0.123). SHAP analysis identified age, BMI, and physical activity as primary risk drivers. Populations with highest diabetes risk receive the worst algorithmic performance, underscoring the need for fairness-aware, age-stratified deployment strategies before clinical use.

</details>


### [408] [More Than Memory: Task-Conditioned Signed FFN Writes in Long-Context Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16254)
*Zhibo Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The study investigates the behavior of Feedforward Networks (FFNs) in long-context retrieval tasks, observing that FFN responses are layer-specific and affect retrieval outcomes. Key findings include the identification of suppressor and amplifier roles among layers and the development of a diagnostic based on write-gradient alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the role of native residual writes in FFNs during retrieval tasks and how these writes influence the retrieval state, particularly in long-context scenarios.

Method: The researchers analyzed the response surfaces of FFNs by scaling the model's writes one layer at a time, examining the outcomes in controlled retrieval tasks without altering weights or introducing external vectors.

Result: They found that FFNs display layer-specific roles, with the final layer serving as a suppressor in 7 out of 8 cases, and approximately 60% of layers switching roles depending on the retrieval mode. The study's diagnostic method effectively predicted retrieval performance outcomes.

Conclusion: Native FFN scaling reveals a structured, task-specific behavior in retrieval processes, with write-gradient alignment serving as an effective diagnostic tool for distinguishing between suppressor and amplifier roles in FFNs.

Abstract: FFNs are often treated as parametric memories. In long-context retrieval, however, the sharper question is not only what they store, but whether their native residual writes push the current retrieval state toward or away from the correct answer. We test this by scaling the model's own FFN write one layer at a time, without editing weights or injecting external steering vectors.
  Across controlled literal and semantic retrieval suites, native FFN response surfaces are signed, layer-specific, and task-conditioned: the final FFN is a suppressor in 7 of 8 model-suite cases, and 60% of layers switch role between retrieval modes (95% CI [50%, 69%]). A local directional derivative along the native write separates the two monotone roles: suppressors have negative derivative in 34/35 cases, and amplifiers have positive derivative in 18/18 cases, so the roles are not reducible to write size. On a safety-filtered LongBench retrieval-QA probe, the same diagnostic predicts attenuation damage with raw R^2=0.796 on Qwen2.5-7B and 0.791 on Qwen3.5-9B; a held-out suppressor-attenuation policy improves retrieval margins over random and norm-matched controls. These results show that native FFN scaling exposes a signed, task-conditioned residual-write structure in retrieval, and that write-gradient alignment is a compact diagnostic for the two monotone roles.

</details>


### [409] [Feature Generation Using LLMs: An Evolutionary Algorithm Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16255)
*Aria Nourbakhsh,Benoît Alcaraz,Christoph Schommer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper explores the use of Large Language Models for feature generation in machine learning, enhancing the process through effective attribute selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve feature engineering in machine learning pipelines, particularly in generating relevant features from tabular data using advanced language models.

Method: The authors developed a pipeline that incorporates an LLM to generate new features based on existing attributes, followed by a selection algorithm to identify the most effective feature sets.

Result: The approach was tested on eight datasets across various domains, demonstrating that the LLM could effectively create new, useful features using mathematical and logical operations, improving classification outcomes in most cases.

Conclusion: The study concludes that LLMs can significantly enhance feature generation processes, strengthening machine learning model performance.

Abstract: A crucial step in machine learning pipelines is to present each entity with features or attributes that are representative of the characteristics of the processed entities. Feature engineering is an important step in finding a relation among attributes that otherwise may not be processed by the ML algorithms. Meanwhile, Large Language Models have shown promising abilities in coding, mathematical reasoning, and processing world knowledge. In this work, we utilize an LLM for the problem of feature generation from tabular data based on the previously given features. We have created a pipeline that takes a set of attributes and a prompt to generate new features. Then, our selection algorithm selects the best-performing sets of attributes. We apply our method to eight datasets from different domains and data types. Our results show that, in most cases, the language model can produce new features based on mathematical and logical operators that are useful for the given tasks and can improve classification results.

</details>


### [410] [From Outcomes to Actions: Leveraging Hindsight for Long-Horizon Language Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16257)
*Zishang Jiang,Tingyun Li,Jinyi Han,Xinyi Wang,Sihang Jiang,Yizhou Ying,Xiaojun Meng,Jiansheng Wei,Jiaqing Liang,Yanghua Xiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Hindsight Policy Optimization (HPO), a new method for reinforcement learning that reduces optimization variance in long-horizon tasks by utilizing an intent space for better signal extraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses challenges in training RL agents for long-horizon interactions, particularly the difficulty in evaluating the impact of actions, which contributes to high optimization variance.

Method: HPO projects current and hindsight policy distributions into an intent space and uses the Wasserstein distance to derive low-variance learning signals.

Result: The paper demonstrates both theoretically and empirically that aggregating semantically similar states and actions in the intent space leads to a more stable policy performance with reduced variance in estimators.
