Result: RGMR demonstrated consistent performance improvements, significantly lowering test-set MSE for drought forecasts, achieving up to an 18.9% reduction in SPEI MSE in South Australia and smaller improvements in other regions.

Conclusion: RGMR offers an efficient method to utilize pre-existing TSFMs for improved regional climate forecasts, enhancing the practical implementation of these models in climate prediction workflows.

Abstract: Regional climate prediction presents unique challenges for time series foundation models, which typically process temporal patterns through single-pass inference. Expert climatologists, in contrast, employ multi-scale temporal analysis and iterative refinement based on systematic error diagnosis. We present RGMR (Residual-Guided Multi-Resolution Refinement), an inference-time framework that adapts pre-trained foundation models to perform structured coarse-to-fine refinement for climate forecasting without updating backbone parameters. Applied to drought forecasting using the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), RGMR is architecture-agnostic across the three TSFM backbones evaluated per site (TimesFM, TimeGPT, TabPFN) and consistently lowers test-set MSE on three South Australian sites and three additional regions outside South Australia. Applied to TimesFM, the wrapper reduces one-month-ahead SPEI MSE by up to 18.9\% across the three South Australian sites (mean reduction $\approx$18.7\%). Overall, RGMR provides a practical route for deploying frozen TSFMs in regional climate forecasting workflows.

</details>


### [499] [Retrieval-Augmented Interpretable Learning: Towards Task-Specific Zero-Shot Models in Healthcare](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17508)
*Sazan Mahbub,Caleb Ellington,Zhiyuan Li,Yixin Yang,Souvik Kundu,Ben Lengerich,Eric P. Xing*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RAIL is a meta-learning framework for creating interpretable models for clinical predictions, utilizing previous tasks to enhance model performance with feature-level explanations and uncertainty quantification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create interpretable and reliable predictive models in healthcare, especially for long-tailed clinical tasks requiring adaptability and human oversight.

Method: RAIL employs a probabilistic meta-learning approach that retrieves and transfers structure from related tasks to generate new predictors in diagnostic-feature space, emphasizing zero-shot and few-shot learning capabilities.

Result: RAIL achieves 73.4% accuracy in zero-shot settings and 73.2% in few-shot settings, outperforming traditional supervised models which struggle in these scenarios.

Conclusion: RAIL presents a viable solution for scalable, interpretable clinical prediction systems, enabling adaptation to new tasks while ensuring model transparency and reliability.

Abstract: We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Interpretable Learning (RAIL), a probabilistic meta-learning framework for zero-shot generation of task-specific interpretable models that synthesizes coefficient-space structure from natural-language task descriptions and a memory of previously learned task-specific predictors. RAIL retrieves related source tasks, transfers structure through coefficient space, and generates a new predictor in the original diagnostic-feature space, enabling zero-shot and few-shot clinical procedure prediction with feature-level explanations. Its probabilistic formulation provides uncertainty over retrieval, model coefficients, and predictions, supporting reliability-aware deployment: uncertain predictions or unstable explanations can be flagged for additional clinical review rather than treated as automatic decisions. This makes RAIL particularly suited for healthcare settings, where prediction tasks are highly long-tailed, new clinical targets arise frequently, and models must remain inspectable, uncertainty-aware, and compatible with human oversight. Across long-tailed clinical procedure prediction tasks, RAIL maintains reliable performance across data-availability regimes: it achieves 73.4% accuracy in the held-out zero-shot settings, where no supervised task-specific model can be trained, and remains near 73.2% accuracy in the extreme few-shot regime with only 2-4 examples, where supervised task-specific models perform close to chance. RAIL further benefits from clinically informed task representations and yields retrieval, uncertainty, and coefficient-level diagnostics that make model behavior more transparent. These results suggest a path toward scalable clinical prediction systems that can adapt to new tasks while preserving interpretability and reliability.

</details>


### [500] [Lightweight Wrappers for Adapting Time Series Foundation Models to Regional Drought Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17511)
*Wentao Gao,Jiuyong Li,Lin Liu,Thuc Duy Le,Jixue Liu,Yanchang Zhao,Yun Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a lightweight adaptation framework for enhancing zero-shot forecasting from Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) without requiring access to model weights, specifically for regional climate forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to overcome challenges like proprietary model weights, limited local data, and constrained computational budgets that hinder traditional fine-tuning in regional climate forecasting.

Method: The proposed framework uses two wrappers: SMR² for multi-resolution temporal decomposition and regional dynamics adaptation, and MBB for block resampling of temporal dependencies, allowing for inference-time adaptation without weight updates.

Result: The framework significantly improves one-month-ahead SPEI predictions, achieving up to 26% reduction in mean squared error across various sites in South Australia.

Conclusion: The lightweight adaptation framework enhances the forecasting performance of TSFMs in resource-constrained environments, demonstrating its practical applicability for regional forecasting systems.

Abstract: Large \emph{Time Series Foundation Models} (TSFMs) demonstrate strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities across diverse domains. However, their application to regional climate forecasting faces practical challenges: model weights are often proprietary, local training records are limited, and computational budgets are constrained, making traditional fine-tuning approaches infeasible. To address these constraints, we introduce a lightweight, black-box adaptation framework (requiring no access to backbone parameters and no backbone fine-tuning) that enhances frozen TSFMs at inference time through two plug-and-play wrappers: \textbf{SMR\textsuperscript{2}} (Stationarity aware multi-resolution Residual), which decomposes the input into multi-resolution temporal views, learns stride specific residual corrections that capture regional dynamics, then adaptively ensembles them into a single forecast, and \textbf{MBB} (Moving Block Bootstrap), which preserves temporal dependencies through block resampling and ensembles over temporally coherent residual perturbations to stabilize the point forecast. Both wrappers instantiate the same bagging style principle: they build diverse views of the input or its residuals, forecast each with the same frozen backbone, and aggregate, so all adaptation comes from inference time ensembling rather than any weight update. Evaluated on one month ahead Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) prediction across multiple sites in South Australia, our framework consistently improves forecasting performance across several backbone models, demonstrating up to 26\% mean squared error (MSE) reduction over the corresponding frozen backbone while enabling practical deployment in resource constrained regional forecasting systems.

</details>


### [501] [One-step lowest-variance selection in a Gaussian random-field model motivated by masked diffusion: Total correlation and a square root collision threshold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17522)
*Linjun Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper examines a selection step in Gaussian random-field models, focusing on confidence-guided parallel unmasking in masked discrete diffusion. It establishes how low-score positions affect selection dependence costs, with two key results regarding Gaussian total correlation at various scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to understand the impact of geometry of low-score locations on dependence costs in parallel decoding within masked discrete diffusion frameworks.

Method: A Gaussian random-field model with a nonnegative score field is used to analyze position selection based on minimal scores and to measure position dependence through a distance-dependent Gaussian correlation model.

Result: Two complementary results are established: conditional Gaussian total correlation vanishes in probability for a sub-square-root regime, while it remains non-negligible with positive asymptotic probability at the square-root scale, along with a positive expectation lower bound.

Conclusion: The findings offer a foundational understanding of the interplay between budget size, score dependence, and spatial correlation in confidence-based selection processes.

Abstract: Motivated by confidence-guided parallel unmasking in masked discrete diffusion, we study a single selection step in a stylized Gaussian random-field model. A locally dependent nonnegative score field represents position wise uncertainty, and the scheduler selects the K positions with the smallest scores. Dependence among the selected positions is measured through a distance-dependent Gaussian correlation model. This separation provides a tractable framework for quantifying how the geometry of low-score locations affects the dependence cost of factorized parallel decoding. We establish two complementary results. In a conservative sub-square-root regime, the conditional Gaussian total correlation of the selected block vanishes in probability. At the square-root scale, it remains non-negligible with positive asymptotic probability and admits a strictly positive expectation lower bound. Synthetic experiments support the predicted finite-size behavior. These results provide a rigorous stochastic-geometry baseline for understanding how budget size, score dependence, and spatial correlation jointly shape one-step confidence-based selection in masked discrete diffusion.

</details>


### [502] [Program Synthesis for Simulation-Based Inference: Joint Model Selection and Parameter Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17540)
*Siddharth Mishra-Sharma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a framework combining large language models with neural simulation-based inference for model selection and parameter estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve parameter estimation for complex models without being restricted to fixed model structures.

Method: Utilizes large language models to generate and refine simulator programs from natural language descriptions, which are then evaluated using neural density estimation.

Result: Successfully identifies plausible model families across various benchmarks, reflecting the data's information content and model identifiability.

Conclusion: The framework enables flexible simulation-based inference, expanding beyond fixed models to a variety of plausible candidate models.

Abstract: Neural simulation-based inference enables parameter estimation for complex models, but typically requires the user to specify a simulator encoding a fixed model structure. We present a framework for joint model selection and parameter estimation that combines large language models for program synthesis with neural simulation-based inference. Given a natural language description of the system and data under investigation, an LLM proposes candidate simulator programs which are iteratively refined via feedback-driven mutation and evaluated using neural density estimation. The approach enables simulation-based inference over a pool of models, not just parameters within a fixed model. On benchmarks spanning deterministic dynamics, stochastic epidemic models, and dark matter substructure inference from gravitational-lensing images, the method identifies plausible model families from open-ended prompts, with accuracy that reflects the information content of the data and identifiability of candidate models.

</details>


### [503] [Volatility-Aware Extreme Event Detection in High-Frequency Financial Markets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17555)
*Maorufa Zaman,Haris Md Sahed*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study develops a volatility-aware method for detecting extreme price movements in high-frequency Bitcoin markets, significantly improving event detection performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address challenges in detecting rare but impactful price movements in financial markets due to non-stationarity and class imbalance using conventional models.

Method: The study proposes a new target formulation that considers both large future returns and high-volatility regimes, employing a tree-based model (XGBoost) with time-series cross-validation.

Result: The method achieves a Precision-Recall AUC of approximately 0.40, surpassing the baseline PR-AUC of around 0.06, indicating a sixfold improvement in rare event detection.

Conclusion: The findings emphasize the importance of target design in financial machine learning, suggesting that incorporating volatility into the labeling enhances detection performance.

Abstract: Predicting extreme price movements in high-frequency financial markets is a challenging task due to non-stationarity, heavy-tailed return distributions, and severe class imbalance. In particular, rare but impactful events are often difficult to detect using conventional modeling approaches, which typically treat extreme movements as isolated observations. This study proposes a volatility-aware approach for extreme event detection using high-frequency Bitcoin limit order book (LOB) data. Motivated by empirical evidence of volatility clustering, the target formulation is extended to incorporate both large future returns and high-volatility regimes. This redefinition increases the proportion of informative samples and aligns the learning objective with the underlying market dynamics. Using a tree-based model (XGBoost) with time-series cross-validation and imbalance-aware evaluation, the proposed method achieves a Precision-Recall AUC of approximately 0.40, significantly outperforming the baseline formulation with a PR-AUC of around 0.06. This represents more than a sixfold improvement in detecting rare events. The results highlight that target design plays a critical role in financial machine learning, often exceeding the impact of model complexity. By incorporating volatility structure into the labeling process, the proposed approach provides a more effective and realistic framework for extreme event detection in high-frequency cryptocurrency markets.

</details>


### [504] [CoCurve: Cross-Module Co-Pruning Curvature for Training-Free Structured LLM Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17568)
*Zhiren Gong,Zihao Zeng,Zijie Wang,Tiantong Wang,Chau Yuen,Wei Yang Bryan Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoCurve introduces a method for structured pruning of language models, addressing unit interdependencies through a Fisher matrix approach to improve efficiency in unit removal without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current training-free pruning methods mismanage the dependency among computational units in Transformers, leading to suboptimal pruning outcomes.

Method: CoCurve employs a calibration-only method based on a second-order Taylor expansion of KL divergence, using a Fisher matrix for assessing unit interdependencies and allowing joint pruning of attention and FFN units efficiently.

Result: The method produces a single quadratic program for pruning that accounts for inter-unit relationships and avoids the need for fine-tuning or additional labels.

Conclusion: CoCurve effectively enhances structured pruning by recognizing and incorporating the interactions between units, leading to improved model compression without extensive retraining.

Abstract: Structured pruning compresses large language models (LLMs) by removing whole computational units, such as attention heads and feed-forward (FFN) channel groups. Most training-free methods, however, rank these units independently, implicitly treating the loss from pruning a set as the sum of its individual losses. This view fails for Transformers, whose sublayers are coupled through a shared residual stream. Two individually weak units can thus be jointly indispensable, yet independent scoring is blind to such dependence and removes them together. We introduce CoCurve (Cross-Module Co-Pruning Curvature), a calibration-only, fine-tuning-free method that prunes attention and FFN units jointly. A second-order Taylor expansion of the token-level KL between the frozen model and its masked copy yields a single Fisher matrix whose diagonal is classical node saliency and whose off-diagonal entries are co-pruning curvature edges: the extra damage of removing two units together. Under a single-ablation additivity approximation this matrix reduces to a Gram product of single-unit ablation features, so the full M x M interaction is recovered from M forward passes, with no pairwise sweeps or gradients. Pruning then reduces to one budgeted quadratic program, solved in a single shot under a shared attention--FFN budget, with no labels, fine-tuning, or recovery.

</details>


### [505] [A Weisfeiler-Leman Characterization of Global-Attention Graph Transformers for Mixed-Integer Linear Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17570)
*Md Abrar Jahin,Craig A. Knoblock,Jay Pujara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper examines the expressive power of graph foundation models (GFMs) in representing mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) through the lens of graph isomorphism testing, particularly focusing on 1-WL equivalence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore the limitations of GFMs with global attention in accurately representing different MILP instances, challenging the idea that these models can always capture deeper structural differences.

Method: The authors apply the 1-WL graph isomorphism test to assess the embeddings generated by hierarchical graph transformers, demonstrating that these embeddings yield identical representations for 1-WL-equivalent graphs, employing various architectures.

Result: The study shows that all tested GFMs, regardless of architecture and settings, produce identical embeddings for non-isomorphic graphs that are 1-WL equivalent, indicating substantial expressiveness limitations.

Conclusion: The findings reveal that while GFMs exhibit some level of expressiveness beyond 1-WL equivalence, this is reliant on input encoding techniques rather than the attention mechanism itself.

Abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) with global attention are increasingly used to represent mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), aiming to capture structure beyond the locality of standard graph neural networks. We study their expressive power through graph isomorphism testing, asking which MILP instances they map to identical representations. We prove that a broad class of hierarchical graph transformers combining global linear attention, edge-weighted cross-attention, and bipartite message passing is bounded by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) test: under any parameter setting, 1-WL-equivalent MILP graphs receive identical graph embeddings. Our compositional proof shows that each architectural component is a symmetric multiset function and thus preserves 1-WL equivalence. We validate this characterization across ten diverse graph encoders, including Graphormer-, GraphGPS-, Set-Transformer-, and Gasse-style models. Across model capacities, graph scales, and pooling operators, every tested encoder maps 1-WL-equivalent non-isomorphic graph pairs to numerically identical embeddings. Consequently, graph invariants that vary within a 1-WL equivalence class cannot be recovered from these representations. We further show that expressiveness beyond 1-WL arises from input encoding rather than attention: random-walk positional encodings separate the constructed pairs, while additional constructions expose the limits of this remedy. These results characterize the expressive power of global-attention GFMs and provide an encoder-agnostic diagnostic for detecting 1-WL-induced representation equivalence.

</details>


### [506] [AGG: Jacobian-Aggregated Group Gradient for Efficient GRPO Training of Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17572)
*Ruiyi Ding,Jie Li,He Kang,Ziyan Liu,Chengru Song,Yuan chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JAGG is a new method that enhances GRPO in training diffusion models, significantly speeding up the backward-pass process while maintaining quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the computational challenges faced by GRPO when applied to high-resolution T2I training, particularly the costly backward-pass through large models.

Method: JAGG uses Jacobian aggregation and t-weighted interpolation of endpoint Jacobians to reduce the number of backward passes needed during training from W to 2 per group of W steps.

Result: An experimental evaluation showed JAGG achieves approximately 2× speedup in backward computation without significant loss of model quality.

Conclusion: JAGG effectively reduces training costs for GRPO in T2I tasks by leveraging the smooth and linear variation of model states.

Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a powerful reinforcement learning algorithm for aligning generative models with human preferences. While successful in large language models~\cite{shao2024deepseekmathpushinglimitsmathematical}, its extension to diffusion and flow matching models introduces a severe computational bottleneck: gradients must be back-propagated through the high-capacity DiT backbone at \emph{every} timestep of the sampling trajectory, making high-resolution text-to-image (T2I) training prohibitively expensive. Training-free DiT inference acceleration methods (e.g., $Δ$-DiT, ScalingCache) exploit the fact that DiT hidden states and velocity predictions vary \emph{smoothly and nearly linearly} along the trajectory. We ask whether the same linearity can reduce the backward-pass cost of DiT RL training, and answer affirmatively with \textbf{JAGG} (\textbf{J}acobian-\textbf{A}ggregated \textbf{G}roup \textbf{G}radient), which reduces full transformer backward passes from $W$ to $2$ per group of $W$ consecutive steps. JAGG approximates intermediate-step Jacobians via $t$-weighted interpolation of the endpoint Jacobians, then aggregates per-step upstream signals into two composite gradients applied through a single joint backward pass. We prove this interpolation is \emph{exact} when the velocity is linear in $(z,t)$, and a cosine-similarity routing rule (\texttt{jagg\_frac}) deploys JAGG only where the assumption holds. Experiments on T2I benchmarks show JAGG delivers $\sim$2$\times$ backward speedup with negligible quality degradation.

</details>


### [507] [Concentration and Mean-Square Bounds for Contractive Stochastic Approximation: A Unified Elementary Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17595)
*Siddharth Chandak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper provides means to analyze stochastic approximation with arbitrary norm contractive mappings under multiplicative noise, yielding mean-square and concentration bounds through a unified approach without smoothing techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address challenges in stochastic approximation, particularly in reinforcement learning, where iterates are unbounded and noise is multiplicative and norm-dependent.

Method: Utilizes an averaged noise sequence with auxiliary iterates to derive a Lyapunov drift inequality for normed error, coupled with induction arguments for both mean-square and concentration bounds.

Result: Establishes the first sub-Gaussian tailed maximal concentration bound for stochastic approximation in the presence of affine multiplicative noise, with a logarithmic dependence of the stepsize on confidence.

Conclusion: The proposed methods are versatile, potentially applicable to various noise models and iterative algorithms beyond the specific scenario analyzed.

Abstract: We establish mean-square and concentration bounds for stochastic approximation (SA) with arbitrary norm contractive mappings, under a multiplicative noise model where the noise may scale affinely with the norm of the iterates, and the iterates are potentially unbounded. These settings arise in reinforcement learning, where operators are often contractive in the $\ell_\infty$ norm and the noise scales with the iterates. To address the arbitrary norm, earlier works replace the non-smooth squared norm with a smooth Lyapunov function constructed via the generalized Moreau envelope. For concentration analysis, these works handle multiplicative noise and unbounded iterates through a multi-stage bootstrapping argument that starts from a time-varying worst-case bound and iteratively refines it. We instead present a unified and elementary analysis that yields both bounds. Using an averaged noise sequence and corresponding auxiliary iterates, we obtain a one-step Lyapunov drift inequality for the normed error directly, without smoothing the norm or constructing an envelope. For the mean-square bound, we combine this drift inequality with an induction argument showing that the iterates remain bounded in expectation. For the concentration bound, we develop a probabilistic induction over a sequence of "good" events on which the iterates are controlled, allowing the standard Azuma-Hoeffding bound to be applied. Our approach yields the first sub-Gaussian tailed maximal (all-time) concentration bound for SA under multiplicative noise, by allowing the stepsize to depend logarithmically on the confidence level. Beyond the specific setting considered here, we discuss the generalizability of these proof techniques to other noise models and iterative algorithms.

</details>


### [508] [Trustworthy Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction via Reliability-Aware Multi-Engine Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17601)
*Yongchan Hong,Defu Cao,Wenjin Liu,Thomas Ku,Jordy Homing Lam,Emily Nguyen,Willie Neiswanger,Vsevolod Katritch,Yan Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RELIABLE-BA is a novel framework for accurate protein-ligand binding affinity prediction that incorporates uncertainty measures, enhancing drug discovery processes. It combines multiple docking engine predictions with a focus on contextual reliability and uncertainty decomposition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for reliable protein-ligand binding affinity predictions in drug discovery, as existing methods lack interpretability and do not account for chemical context.

Method: RELIABLE-BA employs an evidential framework involving three steps: modeling each docking engine as an expert, incorporating learned reliability based on molecular context, and aggregating predictions to account for uncertainty and disagreements among engines.

Result: Experiments show improved prediction accuracy and uncertainty calibration on standard datasets, with the method allowing for more effective filtering of predictions, resulting in a potential 25% reduction in error for retained high-confidence predictions.

Conclusion: RELIABLE-BA is the first framework to effectively merge evidential fusion with context-dependent reliability, enhancing the trustworthiness of AI-guided drug discovery.

Abstract: Accurate protein-ligand binding affinity prediction is central to computational drug discovery, yet modern docking engines frequently disagree without indicating which prediction to trust. Consensus scoring and ensemble methods improve mean accuracy but treat all predictions identically without interpretable confidence measures or uncertainty decomposition, ignoring the chemical context of each protein-ligand pair. To address this limitation, we introduce RELIABLE-BA (RELIABiLity-aware Evidential fusion for Binding Affinity), an evidential framework for multi-engine binding affinity prediction. Our model comprises three steps: (1) modeling each engine as an evidential expert via Normal-Inverse-Gamma distributions, (2) scaling epistemic uncertainty through learned reliability from molecular context while preserving each expert's predictive mean, and (3) fusing experts through closed-form aggregation that captures both individual uncertainty and inter-engine disagreement. Experiments on the PDBBind and BDB2020+ benchmarks demonstrate competitive point prediction with substantially improved uncertainty calibration, and additional validation on the SARS-CoV-2 Mpro dataset and 5HT2A receptor demonstrates applicability to clinically relevant drug targets. Crucially, these uncertainty estimates enable reliable filtering of protein-ligand pairs, reducing prediction error by up to 25% when retaining only high-confidence pairs. To our knowledge, RELIABLE-BA is the first multi-engine binding affinity prediction framework to combine evidential fusion with context-dependent reliability, offering a principled path toward trustworthy AI-guided drug discovery. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yongchand/RELIABLE-BA.

</details>


### [509] [Optimizing the Preconditioner: A Black-box Online-to-Nonconvex Conversion with Static Regret Minimization Oracles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17607)
*Haichen Hu,David Simchi-Levi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether stochastic nonconvex optimization can be framed as static regret minimization in online convex optimization, providing a black-box approach that leads to improved convergence rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses the challenge of optimizing nonconvex functions by proposing a method that links stochastic optimization to established online learning frameworks, thereby enhancing the understanding and performance of online optimization algorithms.

Method: The authors implement a reduction that utilizes a gradient tracker within a black-box structure where an online learner selects a preconditioner. They analyze performance against linear convex losses and compare it to fixed comparators in an online game setting.

Result: They establish convergence bounds demonstrating that a black-box OCO algorithm with an appropriate static-regret characteristic can achieve optimal convergence rates, even for Lipschitz nonconvex objectives without smooth gradients.

Conclusion: The paper asserts that the proposed framework not only resolves existing open problems in the field but also redefines how optimization algorithms can be conceptualized, emphasizing the separation of gradient prediction and preconditioner selection in adaptive optimization.

Abstract: We study whether stochastic nonconvex optimization can be reduced to ordinary static regret minimization in online convex optimization in a black-box manner. For smooth nonconvex objectives, our reduction maintains a predictable gradient tracker, while a black-box online learner selects a preconditioner that determines how this tracker is transformed into the update direction. The learner receives linear convex losses and is evaluated against a single fixed comparator over one undiscounted online game. For a $β$-smooth objective with range bounded by $M$ and an unbiased stochastic-gradient oracle with variance bounded by \(σ^2\), we establish $$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T
  \mathbb E\!\left[\|\nabla f(x_t)\|_2^2\right]
  \lesssim
  \frac{σ\sqrt{Mβ}}{\sqrt T}
  +
  \frac{\sqrt{Mβ}\,
  \mathscr R_T(\mathcal A,I_d)}{T}
  +
  \frac{Mβ}{T}.$$ Consequently, any black-box OCO algorithm with $\mathscr R_T(\mathcal A,I_d)=O(\sqrt T)$ recovers the classical $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ convergence rate.
  We further show that the same black-box framework extends beyond the smooth setting to Lipschitz nonconvex objectives without Lipschitz continuous gradients. Importantly, this extension continues to rely only on an ordinary static-regret guarantee and requires no stronger notion of online regret. When the OCO oracle admits square-root static regret, the resulting conversion achieves the optimal $O(T^{-2/7})$ convergence rate for the corresponding Goldstein stationary point. These results resolve the open problem posed by Chen and Hazan (2024). More broadly, our framework separates optimizer design into gradient prediction and online preconditioner selection, providing a principled perspective on how adaptive optimization methods such as AdaGrad and Shampoo may be understood through static regret and applied in nonconvex optimization.

</details>


### [510] [Can Transformers Really Do It All? On the Compatibility of Inductive Biases Across Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17624)
*Damien Teney,Liangze Jiang,Hemanth Saratchandran,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates optimizing transformer architectures for specific tasks, revealing that task-specific designs can outperform standard transformers in certain scenarios while highlighting the trade-off between specialization and universality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore if transformers can be optimized for specific tasks or datasets to enhance AI performance beyond mere scaling.

Method: The study introduces a method that replaces key non-linearities in transformers with functions learned from held-out data, allowing for task-specific architecture optimization.

Result: The approach yielded new architectures that showed significant gains in learning speed and generalization for toy tasks, while also identifying designs that performed better for specific datasets in code and language modeling.

Conclusion: Standard transformers often do not represent the best architectural choice for specific tasks, suggesting potential for further advancements in multi-capability architectures.

Abstract: Transformers are remarkably versatile and their design is largely consistent across a variety of applications. But are they optimal for any given task or dataset? The answer may be key for pushing AI beyond merely scaling current designs.
  *Method.* We present a method to optimize a transformer architecture for a given dataset, which we use as a tool to study optimal task-specific inductive biases. This method replaces the most important non-linearities (GeLUs,;softmax) with functions learned on held-out data. We then train the resulting architectures on other datasets, as a way to evaluate the compatibility between pairs of tasks.
  Findings. On algorithmic toy tasks, we identify new architectures with dramatic improvements in learning speed, in- and out-of-distribution generalization, and stability across seeds. The new designs prove very task-specific however, and indicate that these tasks require inductive biases very different from those of standard transformers. On code and language modeling datasets, we also find architectures with consistent, yet smaller improvements. These designs transfer much better across datasets and domains (English & computer code).
  Implications. Our results show that standard transformers are rarely a local optimum in the space of architectures. Simple alternatives can perform much better but sacrifice universality. This suggests that there may be room for improved architectures that better support multiple capabilities simultaneously, such as fluency and robust reasoning.

</details>


### [511] [TypiCore: A Hybrid Active Query Strategy for Class-Incremental Learning on Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17632)
*Gabor Szucs,Samuel Jacsev,Marcell Nemeth,Davide Dalle Pezze,Gian Antonio Susto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper explores Active Class-Incremental Learning (ACIL) for multivariate time series, focusing on efficient label querying under budget constraints, proposing a new strategy called TypiCore that improves model performance and label efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for effective learning from partially labeled time series data within real-world distribution shifts, while managing the costs of labeling.

Method: The paper assesses various query strategies paired with rehearsal-based techniques, focusing on their impact on learning metrics, and introduces TypiCore as a hybrid approach for sample selection.

Result: TypiCore significantly outperforms existing methods and approaches the performance of fully supervised learning with considerably fewer labels across multiple datasets.

Conclusion: TypiCore enhances label efficiency and model performance in Active Class-Incremental Learning for time series data, overcoming limitations of previous methods under budget constraints.

Abstract: Time series data play a pivotal role across numerous domains, including healthcare and manufacturing. In real-world environments, models must cope with distribution shifts over time, a challenge commonly addressed through Continual Learning (CL) techniques. However, existing CL methods face a critical limitation: real-world data streams are rarely fully labeled, making annotation cost a major practical constraint. This paper investigates Active Class-Incremental Learning (ACIL) for multivariate time series, where a model must sequentially learn new classes while selectively querying labels under a fixed annotation budget. We present a systematic evaluation of a wide range of query strategies combined with multiple rehearsal-based approaches, assessing their impact on plasticity, stability, and label efficiency across four benchmark datasets. Our analysis reveals the limitations of uncertainty-based and distribution-aware methods in achieving strong performance under constrained labeling budgets. To address these shortcomings, we propose TypiCore, a novel hybrid query strategy that alternates between typicality-based and diversity-based sample selection across active learning cycles, enabling the construction of memory buffers that are both representative and diverse. Evaluated on the TSCIL benchmark, TypiCore delivers statistically significant improvements over all baselines and matches or surpasses fully supervised continual learning performance on multiple datasets while requiring a fraction of the available labels.

</details>


### [512] [Selectivity Matters: Source Node Influence Pruning for Unsupervised Graph Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17668)
*Ridong Han,Yawen Shen,Zhongnian Li,Tongfeng Sun,Xinzheng Xu,Abdulmotaleb El Saddik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents Source Node Influence Pruning (SNIP), a method for improving unsupervised graph domain adaptation by selectively utilizing source nodes to avoid noise from structurally incompatible nodes, leading to enhanced performance through better alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The goal is to enhance unsupervised graph domain adaptation (UGDA) by addressing the limitations of existing node-level alignment methods that assume all source nodes are beneficial, which can introduce noise due to structural shifts.

Method: SNIP quantifies structural discrepancies using centrality measures to assign influence scores to source nodes, filtering out those with low scores to create a refined 'sub-source' graph.

Result: Experiments across eight transfer scenarios on five datasets demonstrate that SNIP surpasses existing methods, confirming the benefit of selective node utilization for adaptation.

Conclusion: Selective source node utilization via SNIP leads to superior adaptation performance in graph domain transfer tasks compared to traditional full-graph approaches.

Abstract: Unsupervised Graph Domain Adaptation (UGDA) aims to facilitate knowledge transfer from a labeled source graph to an unlabeled target graph by mitigating cross-domain distribution shifts. Existing methods primarily focus on node-level feature alignment in latent spaces, relying on the implicit assumption that all source nodes contribute positively to the alignment. However, this assumption often fails because a node's semantic information is intrinsically coupled with its topological graph structure. Due to structural shifts, source nodes with severe structural deviations (e.g., structural outliers) lack semantic counterparts in the target graph, and forcing alignment on them introduces severe noise and causes negative transfer. To bridge this gap, we argue that selective source node utilization is superior to full-graph training, thereby shifting the research paradigm from feature-level alignment to data-level refinement. To this end, we propose Source Node Influence Pruning (SNIP), a novel model-agnostic, data-centric refinement framework. Specifically, SNIP quantifies the structural discrepancy between individual source nodes and the target domain by integrating multiple centrality measures, assigning each source node an influence score. A rank-based normalization mechanism is further employed to eliminate scale variations across different measures, allowing SNIP to effectively identify and filter out structurally incompatible nodes with low influence scores. As a plug-and-play method, SNIP constructs a refined "sub-source" graph that is inherently more beneficial for subsequent alignment. Comprehensive experiments across eight transfer scenarios on five real-world datasets demonstrate that SNIP consistently outperforms competitive baselines and significantly enhances adaptation performance, validating the superiority of selective node utilization over full-graph training.

</details>


### [513] [GeneSpeak-FP: Target and Compound Retrieval from Observed Cell-Level Perturbation Signatures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17671)
*Kseniia Vaniushkina,Jeongmin Lim,Jinyong Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a Transformer retrieval model designed to identify targets and compounds in a closed-library setting based on observed transcriptional responses from cell-level perturbation signatures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of identifying consistent targets and compounds corresponding to given transcriptional responses in large-scale single-cell perturbation atlases.

Method: The model uses a Transformer architecture where each perturbation signature is compared against a mean DMSO reference, with the encoder producing target-retrieval and molecular-embedding vectors, trained with supervised losses and alignment of structure and transcriptome.

Result: In evaluations, the model achieved notable retrieval metrics with Recall@10 of 0.408, Recall@20 of 0.544, Hit@1 of 0.129, Hit@10 of 0.343, and mean reciprocal rank of 0.205 across 379 compounds.

Conclusion: The results indicate that the multi-task model can effectively recover target annotations and compound identities from cell-level responses; however, further studies are needed to assess generalization to new compounds and cellular contexts.

Abstract: Large-scale single-cell perturbation atlases make it possible to ask an inverse question: given an observed transcriptional response, which annotated targets and compounds in a fixed library are most consistent with that response? We present \model, a Transformer retrieval model for this closed-library setting. Each input is a cell-level perturbation signature formed by contrasting one treated cell with a cell-line-specific mean DMSO reference. The encoder maps the signature to a target-retrieval vector and a molecular-embedding vector, trained jointly with supervised target losses and structure--transcriptome alignment. We evaluate on Tahoe-100M conditions with mapped target annotations using a within-compound stratified 90/10 condition-pair split of 10,505 training and 1,168 validation drug--cell-line pairs. Because compounds and cell lines can occur in both partitions, the experiment measures held-out condition-pair retrieval rather than generalization to unseen compounds or cellular contexts. In a Monte Carlo evaluation over 38,400 sampled validation cells, \model\ achieved target Recall@10 of 0.408 and Recall@20 of 0.544, together with compound Hit@1 of 0.129, Hit@10 of 0.343, and mean reciprocal rank of 0.205 over a 379-compound bank. A separate diagnostic evaluation produced nearly identical values for the main model and large gains over a random-vector control and post-hoc bag-of-genes controls. These results demonstrate that a single multi-task model can recover both mapped target annotations and recorded compound identities from observed cell-level responses in the evaluated Tahoe-100M closed-library setting. Generalization to unseen compounds and cellular contexts remains to be established.

</details>


### [514] [Beyond Objective Expressivity: Geometry Preservation in Multimodal Contrastive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17673)
*Tillmann Rheude,Roland Eils,Benjamin Wild*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper discusses challenges in trimodal contrastive learning and proposes geometry-preserving encoders to enhance optimization through improved Jacobian conditioning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address optimization and representation challenges that arise when extending contrastive learning models to three or more modalities.

Method: The authors introduce geometry-preserving encoders that condition the Jacobian via regularization and implement modifications like LeakyReLU activations and residual paths.

Result: Improving Jacobian conditioning enhances retrieval and linear probe performance across multiple contrastive objectives, particularly in scenarios with missing modalities.

Conclusion: The study highlights the importance of geometric and optimization properties of encoders in multimodal contrastive learning, beyond just the expressivity of objectives.

Abstract: Contrastive learning is increasingly moving toward settings with three or more modalities instead of image-text pairs. Yet, extending models from pairwise to higher-order multimodal alignment can introduce optimization and representation challenges. We identify encoder Jacobian conditioning as a key factor in trimodal contrastive learning: poorly conditioned encoders exhibit collapsing or amplified singular-value spectra, leading to exploding Jacobian condition numbers and degraded multimodal alignment. We introduce geometry-preserving encoders (GPEs) by directly conditioning the Jacobian through regularization and demonstrating that simple modifications like LeakyReLU activations and residual paths recover these geometric benefits. Across a synthetic benchmark and four real-world datasets including missing modalities, improving Jacobian conditioning boosts retrieval and linear probe performance across multiple contrastive objectives, whereas expressive objectives yield little benefit in linear probes. More broadly, our results show that multimodal contrastive learning depends not only on objective expressivity, but also on the geometric and optimization properties of the underlying encoders.

</details>


### [515] [Uncovering Latent Reasoning Strategies in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17674)
*Awni Altabaa,John Lafferty*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a method to decompose the response distribution of a pretrained language model into structured, strategy-conditioned representations, addressing the challenge of posterior collapse with a novel variational objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to understand and decompose the implicit strategies embedded in a language model's responses to reasoning tasks.

Method: The authors introduce a latent-variable factorization approach where a router creates a distribution over latent strategies, and a generator produces responses conditioned on these strategies. A modified variational objective is employed to prevent posterior collapse.

Result: The proposed method successfully recovers latent codes that correspond to distinct reference strategies while maintaining the original model's response capabilities, validated through a benchmark of multi-strategy tasks.

Conclusion: This research provides insights into decomposing response distributions, revealing interpretable strategy-conditioning in language models.

Abstract: A language model $p_θ(y \mid x)$ trained on reasoning tasks learns to solve problems via multiple distinct strategies, yet these strategies are implicit and entangled within the model's response distribution. We study the problem of decomposing the response distribution of a given pretrained language model into a structured, strategy-conditioned representation. Specifically, we learn a latent-variable factorization $p_θ(y \mid x) \leadsto (r_φ(z \mid x), g_φ(y \mid x,z))$, where a router $r$ maps each input to a distribution over latent strategies $z$ and a generator $g$ produces the response conditioned on that strategy. A key challenge is that the generator, initialized from the base model, already represents $p_θ(y \mid x)$ without using $z$. Standard variational inference therefore gives the model no incentive to route information through $z$ and can yield a severe form of posterior collapse. To address this, we propose a variational objective that measures fractional information gain relative to the base model's response loss and concentrates reconstruction pressure on tokens with high base model surprisal, encouraging $z$ to encode strategy-relevant response variation. We introduce a benchmark of multi-strategy algorithmic tasks and show that this objective recovers latent codes aligned with distinct reference strategies while preserving the base model's response distribution.

</details>


### [516] [Planning with Transformers: Chain of Computation and Structured Context Windows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17710)
*Ehsan Futuhi,Nathan R. Sturtevant*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the gap between the theoretical capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and their empirical performance in planning problems, introducing a new architecture called Chain of Computation (COC) that enhances LLMs' planning abilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research aims to bridge the discrepancy between the Turing-completeness of transformers and their underperformance in planning tasks.

Method: The authors propose the Chain of Computation (COC) architecture, which includes a transformer-based language model (LM) within an iterative loop, utilizing a Structured Context Window (SCW) to maintain a manageable context size while enabling adaptive planning.

Result: The COC architecture allows smaller LMs to learn effective planning policies, achieving over 99.89% success rates on BlocksWorld and the Pancake puzzle, and successfully solving the Tower of Hanoi problem with significant action requirements and reduced training data.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate that COC effectively enhances LLMs' planning capabilities, revealing potential for solving complex computational tasks with fewer training instances.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have had a remarkable impact across many areas of machine learning. However, recent studies have shown that they struggle to reliably solve planning problems. At the same time, theoretical results have shown that transformers, the core architecture underlying modern LLMs, are Turing-complete. In this work, we investigate this apparent gap between the theoretical computational power of LLMs and their empirical planning performance. We propose Chain of Computation (COC), a computational architecture that places a transformer-based LM inside an iterative loop, leveraging its strength as a pattern-matching system. The COC uses a Structured Context Window (SCW) which provides a constant-sized context window with support for choosing which window is used at each planning step. Within this architecture, the LM is able to learn a planning policy, predicts the world model, and performs the arithmetic operations required during planning. We show that, when given an append-only SCW (resembling a Turing Machine tape), even relatively small LMs trained from scratch can learn planning policies and generalize from a small number of training instances within each planning domain, achieving success rates above 99.89\% on BlocksWorld and the Pancake puzzle. Our analysis of failure cases in Tower of Hanoi (TOH) reveals that they arise from arithmetic operations or from encountering previously unseen tokens. We show that COC can solve TOH problem instances with up to 20 disks, requiring over 1 million actions, while requiring substantially less training data by either (1) planning with symbolical support for arithmetic or by (2) using a deterministic pushdown automaton (PDA) formulation for the SCW.

</details>


### [517] [MXSens: Sensitivity-Aware Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17733)
*Simla Burcu Harma,Danila Mishin,Zhengyuan Su,Ayan Chakraborty,Elizaveta Kostenok,Dongho Ha,Babak Falsafi,Martin Jaggi,Yunho Oh,Amir Yazdanbakhsh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents MXSens, a mixed mantissa bitwidth method for 4-bit quantization of LLMs, improving accuracy and efficiency by addressing sensitivity to outliers while utilizing hardware-encoded scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To tackle significant accuracy loss in 4-bit quantization due to outliers and inefficiencies in existing methods that rely on software scaling and dequantization.

Method: Introduces MXSens, a training-free approach that assigns variable mantissa bitwidths based on layer and column sensitivity in a block structure, leveraging hardware-based scaling.

Result: MXSens outperforms leading quantization techniques, achieving better perplexities on LLaMA models under the W4A4KV4 setting, particularly on WikiText-2.

Conclusion: The proposed method successfully balances accuracy and resource efficiency in the quantization of large language models.

Abstract: 4-bit quantization enables efficient LLM inference, but suffers from significant accuracy degradation due to outliers. Prior work addresses this problem via data rotation or mixed-precision integer quantization, but often relies on software-managed scaling and frequent dequantization, incurring substantial overhead. Microscaling formats, such as MXINT, eliminate these inefficiencies by encoding scales in hardware, yet remain incompatible with rotation-based methods. Our analysis reveals that outliers vary in severity, from rare extremes to frequent mild deviations, and that quantization sensitivity is unevenly distributed across layers and columns. These insights motivate a fine-grained, sensitivity-guided approach. We introduce MXSens, a training-free method that assigns mixed mantissa bitwidths (4/6/8) based on column- and layer-wise sensitivity, naturally leveraging the block-wise structure of MXINT. MXSens outperforms state-of-the-art quantization methods across a range of models and tasks. Under the W4A4KV4 setting, MXSens achieves perplexities of 3.77 and 7.63 on LLaMA-2-70B and LLaMA-3-8B, respectively, substantially improving over existing baselines on WikiText-2. Our work establishes a new balance between accuracy and resource efficiency for LLM quantization.

</details>


### [518] [Towards Reliable Zero-Shot Crowd Forecasting: Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models for Special Event Pedestrian Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17758)
*Ziteng Li,Yanan Xin,Tina Comes,Serge Hoogendoorn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper explores the use of pretrained time series foundation models for real-time pedestrian-flow forecasting during special events, highlighting the challenges and the importance of probabilistic uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve public safety and operational efficiency during infrequent large-scale events, there is a need for reliable real-time forecasting of pedestrian flows, which is complicated by limited historical data and varying conditions.

Method: The authors investigate the application of pretrained time series foundation models for zero-shot probabilistic forecasting, assessing their performance using decision-oriented metrics in the context of the SAIL2025 event.

Result: The comprehensive assessment reveals the effectiveness of these models in providing reliable forecasts under operational constraints, along with guidelines for their use in crowd management.

Conclusion: The study offers practical recommendations for crowd managers on the conditions under which zero-shot forecasts can be considered operationally reliable.

Abstract: Managing massive crowds during infrequent special events requires reliable real-time pedestrian-flow forecasting to ensure public safety and operational efficiency. However, supervised forecasting methods face limitations in these contexts due to scarce historical data, heterogeneous data distributions, and short in-event observation windows. To effectively support operational decision-making, forecasts should provide not only accurate point estimates but also informative predictive uncertainty. Probabilistic uncertainty quantification plays a critical role in this aspect, particularly capturing sudden volatility and tail risks. This paper investigates pretrained time series foundation models as a lightweight approach for zero-shot probabilistic forecasting without extensive local retraining. Using decision-oriented metrics tailored to short events, we conduct a comprehensive assessment of two time series foundation models on crowd forecasting, with the SAIL2025 event as a use case. We then distill practical insights for crowd managers, specifying when zero-shot forecasts remain operationally reliable.

</details>


### [519] [Feature Attribution-Based Explainability Analysis of Deep Learning Models in Predictive Process Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17783)
*Kseniya Sahatova,Rafael Seidi Oyamada,Xuefei Lu,Johannes De Smedt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a post-hoc explainability method for deep neural networks in predictive process monitoring, addressing challenges in attribution complexity and control-flow dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for trust in deep neural networks for outcome prediction in business processes due to their black-box nature and the limitations of traditional feature attribution methods.

Method: A local post-hoc explainability method that utilizes a control-flow-aware segmentation algorithm to partition event traces into meaningful segments for segment-level SHAP explanations.

Result: The method effectively identifies influential parts of event traces and change points that guide predictions, demonstrated on synthetic and real-world datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed method enhances interpretability in predictive process monitoring, improving trust and practical application of neural networks in business processes.

Abstract: Predictive process monitoring supports the optimization and control of operational business processes by forecasting the future state or outcome of ongoing cases. While deep neural networks have achieved strong performance for these tasks by modeling sequential dependencies in event logs, their black-box nature limits trust and practical adoption. Feature attribution methods are often used to address this, but applying them directly poses a dilemma: event-level attributions impose high computational complexity for long traces, while explanations based on aggregated trace representations often fail to capture the underlying control-flow dynamics. To address this issue, we propose a local post-hoc explainability method for deep neural networks in outcome prediction. The method relies on a control-flow-aware segmentation algorithm that partitions a trace into meaningful segments and supports the computation of segment-level SHAP explanations. This makes it possible to identify which parts of a trace influence a prediction and which change points steer the case toward the predicted outcome. We assess the proposed segmentation method on a synthetic dataset with known process logic, where meaningful change points can be explicitly verified, and we demonstrate its usefulness on real-world event logs from a loan application process and an administrative process of a Dutch municipality.

</details>


### [520] [The Concept of Representation in ML: Beyond Plato and Aristotle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17800)
*Gilad Landau,Aviv Keren*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper explores the concept of representation in machine learning, arguing its philosophical implications, particularly regarding claims of convergence in AI models' representational properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the philosophical implications of representational properties in AI, particularly concerning recent claims about convergence among models.

Method: The authors analyze philosophical debates on mental representation and assess arguments related to The Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

Result: The examination reveals that philosophical insights can help clarify the significance of representational convergence claims and highlight the limitations of alignment evidence.

Conclusion: The paper suggests that deeper philosophical understanding is crucial for interpreting representational properties in AI and outlines future research directions.

Abstract: Representation is a central concept in modern machine learning, where it usually refers to internal encodings that support learning and generalization. As models scale and their capabilities become increasingly human-level, this representational language sometimes shifts from an engineering context into the more philosophically loaded domain of mental representation. We argue that this is the case for recent claims about the convergence of representational properties across different AI models. In particular, we assess the arguments developed in The Platonic Representation Hypothesis, according to which this convergence is driven by a unified structure of reality. We examine this claim by introducing arguments and ideas from debates about mental representation in the philosophy of mind. We argue that these philosophical resources can clarify what is at stake in such claims, explain why alignment evidence alone is insufficient for strong metaphysical conclusions, and suggest directions for future research.

</details>


### [521] [Phasor Attention: Mean Root Square Normalization for Phase Manifold Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17822)
*Sungwoo Goo,Hwi-yeol Yun,Sangkeun Jung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MRSNorm introduces a novel normalization method that enhances stability and efficiency in deep learning models by using geometric constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of Root Mean Square Normalization, which causes numerical instability and gradient issues due to outliers.

Method: MRSNorm pairs channels into 2D phasors, calculating $L_2$ magnitudes locally and averaging globally using $L_1$, thereby constraining activations and halving the number of parameters.

Result: MRSNorm exhibits superior stability in gradients under extreme conditions compared to standard normalization methods, maintaining optimization without divergence.

Conclusion: MRSNorm establishes a new standard for deep representation learning, offering improved structural integrity and efficiency.

Abstract: While Root Mean Square Normalization has become the de facto standard for accelerating modern sequence models, its reliance on the quadratic accumulation of independent scalars ($\sum x^2$) inherently triggers outlier-induced numerical instability, gradient starvation, and anisotropic phase distortion. We introduce Mean Root Square Normalization (MRSNorm). By structurally pairing channels into 2D phasors, MRSNorm mathematically inverts the traditional scaling paradigm: it computes the localized $L_2$ magnitudes (Root Square) before aggregating them via a global $L_1$ average (Mean).
  This operational inversion strictly constrains activations to a phasor manifold, preserving conformal invariance. By sharing a single affine weight across phasor components, MRSNorm halves the total number of learnable parameters, proving that unconstrained spatial scaling in standard norms is a harmful redundancy. We analytically demonstrate that this geometric constraint yields a built-in, trigonometric gradient clipper governed by the Pythagorean identity, unconditionally equalizing the local gradient norm to ensure Gradient Homogeneity.
  Empirical evaluations on a ResNet with CIFAR-100 show that despite halved parameters, MRSNorm provides critical structural stability under rigorous stress tests. Under extreme hyperparameter settings where standard normalizations suffer from gradient divergence, MRSNorm successfully prevents numerical explosion and secures stable optimization trajectories. Our findings propose a fundamental paradigm shift toward phasor-based deep representation learning. The implementation of MRSNorm is available at Appendix C.

</details>


### [522] [Theoretical Foundations of $\max$@$k$ Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17823)
*Riccardo Poiani,Martino Bernasconi,Andrea Celli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates the theoretical aspects of optimizing $	ext{max}@k$ metrics in finite-horizon reinforcement learning, demonstrating its complexity compared to traditional methods and presenting an efficient learning algorithm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limited theoretical understanding of $	ext{max}@k$ learning criteria in reinforcement learning, particularly for challenging applications like code generation and theorem proving.

Method: A theoretical analysis of the $	ext{max}@k$ learning problem, examining the differences between optimizing $	ext{max}@k$ objectives and expected-return maximization, and introducing an efficient algorithm for learning $	ext{max}@k$-optimal policies.

Result: The study shows that Markovian policies are generally inadequate for these objectives, identifies a state augmentation that restores optimality, and reveals a performance gap between different policy types, while highlighting the increased statistical difficulty of learning $	ext{max}@k$-optimal policies.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that $	ext{max}@k$ learning is significantly more complex than standard reinforcement learning, with the proposed algorithm achieving optimal sample complexity to learn effective policies.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning is a cornerstone technique for modern large reasoning models. Usually, for difficult tasks such as code generation and theorem proving, the agent is evaluated by generating $K$ responses rather than sampling a single response, and performance is then measured using a retry-aware metric such as $\max$@$k$. Despite their practical importance, the theoretical foundations of learning under such criteria remain limited. In this work, we provide a theoretical study of the $\max$@$k$ learning problem in finite-horizon reinforcement learning. We show that optimizing the $\max$@$k$ objectives is fundamentally different from standard expected-return maximization. In particular, we prove that Markovian policies are in general insufficient, identify a compact state augmentation that restores optimality, and explicitly characterize the performance gap that can arise between history-dependent and non-history-dependent policies. Moreover, we show that learning $\max$@$k$-optimal policies is statistically harder than standard reinforcement learning and provide an efficient algorithm that achieves the optimal sample complexity rate.

</details>


### [523] [Distributional Soft Bellman Operator under the Cramér Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17897)
*Keru Wang,Yixin Deng,Yao Lyu,Stephen Redmond,Shengbo Eben Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes the fixed-policy distributional soft Bellman operator within the framework of distributional reinforcement learning using Cramér geometry, proving its contraction property and establishing a unique fixed point in the context of maximum-entropy control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to bridge distributional reinforcement learning and maximum-entropy control, focusing on the theoretical foundation through the lens of Cramér geometry.

Method: The authors formulate the CDF-level distributional soft Bellman operator on an admissible CDF field, proving it to be a $ho$-contraction and identifying a unique fixed point via Cramér geometry.

Result: The fixed-policy distributional soft Bellman operator is shown to be a $ho$-contraction under Cramér geometry, leading to a unique fixed point and conditions for convergent iterative policy evaluation.

Conclusion: The findings provide a crucial understanding of the Cramér-geometric Bellman fixed point, essential for improving approximate critics and evaluating critic-loss design in algorithms related to DSPI.

Abstract: Distributional soft policy iteration (DSPI) provides an important framework for combining distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) with maximum-entropy control, in which the policy evaluation step is governed by a distributional soft Bellman operator acting on entropy-regularised returns. Theoretical analysis of such an evaluation step requires a probability metric under which Bellman updates can be controlled, typically by showing that the operator contracts the distance between any two candidate return-distribution estimates. In this paper, we focus on the Cramér geometry, a cumulative distribution function (CDF)-based metric with an $L^2$ structure, and study whether the fixed-policy distributional soft Bellman operator has this contraction property and hence a unique fixed point under this metric. Working directly on an admissible CDF field domain, we formulate the CDF-level distributional soft Bellman operator, prove that it is a $\sqrtγ$-contraction, and obtain the corresponding unique fixed point together with convergent iterative policy evaluation. The CDF formulation also shows that this finite-Cramér-domain property follows from a uniform first-moment condition on the combined one-step reward entropy shift, rather than from separate uniform boundedness assumptions on the reward and entropy terms. We then transport the same evaluation problem to the spectral domain by conjugation, obtaining an equivalent Hilbert-space representation of the same decision process. Taken together, these results identify the Cramér-geometric Bellman fixed point associated with the policy-evaluation step of DSPI, providing a reference point for studying approximate critics, evaluation error, and critic-loss design in DSPI-style algorithms.

</details>


### [524] [The Art of Not Forgetting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17944)
*Ashmith Atmuri,Akshay Kumar,Yashaswini Rao Bhogarajula*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CMP architecture demonstrates superior resistance to catastrophic forgetting compared to backpropagation-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the traditional approach to catastrophic forgetting by proposing that a structural consequence of backpropagation leads to memory issues.

Method: Introduces CMP, which employs sparse relational codes and learns through local, gradient-free updates without backpropagation; tested on a domain-incremental protocol across 15 text domains.

Result: CMP shows a 15-19x improvement in backward transfer compared to a Transformer using online EWC, with a reported accuracy gap.

Conclusion: Local, sparse learning outperforms backpropagation in resisting catastrophic forgetting, with specific conditions stated for validation.

Abstract: We introduce CMP (Cognitive Memory Primitive), an architecture that represents inputs as sparse relational codes, stores them in a two-tier competitive memory, and learns entirely through local, gradient-free updates, with no backpropagation anywhere in the network. We use this architecture to test a specific hypothesis: that catastrophic forgetting, usually treated as a training-time defect to be patched with replay or regularization, is instead a structural consequence of how backpropagation assigns credit and that a learning rule that is local and sparse by construction should resist it without a patch. On a controlled domain-incremental protocol across 15 text domains, three-seed replicated, CMP's backward transfer is 15-19x better than a matched-size Transformer trained with online EWC, and the result survives a domain-order control (reported as a range, +0.24 to +0.44, rather than a single figure). We report this alongside a real, substantial accuracy gap versus the Transformer baseline, a null result on a recognized vision benchmark, and a diagnosed, unresolved failure attempting to combine this architecture with a separate mechanism that improves raw accuracy, disclosed because an honest negative result is more useful than an omitted one. The central claim is narrow and falsifiable: local, sparse, non-backpropagation learning measurably resists catastrophic forgetting better than backpropagation with its standard fix, under conditions we state precisely.

</details>


### [525] [A Geometric Perspective on Stabilizing Value Conflict Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17946)
*Saket Reddy,Andy Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates the use of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to improve Large Language Models' (LLMs) handling of value conflicts linked to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs face issues in navigating value conflicts due to the limitations of scalar rewards from RLHF.

Method: The research examines the impact of CoT reasoning on the model's loss landscape, showing that it helps smoothen the sharpest direction of loss, thus addressing optimization instability. A new value conflict-focused CoT design is created to enhance moral reasoning capabilities.

Result: The CoT approach leads to improved performance on downstream benchmarks related to moral reasoning and demonstrates generalizability across various moral reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: Modifying reasoning dynamics through CoT provides a viable method for improving LLM performance in contexts with complex value conflicts, thereby enhancing pluralistic alignment.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle to navigate value conflicts when trained with the compressed scalar rewards of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). To address this challenge, we investigate how chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can help improve performance in this domain. Geometrically, we show that CoT correlates with further smoothing the model's loss landscape in its sharpest direction, helping resolve the optimization instability of traditional scalar rewards. We also demonstrate via relevant downstream benchmarks that value conflict-focused CoT may generalize to different kinds of moral reasoning, demonstrating that this CoT has the potential to be an effective mechanism for better moral reasoning. To capitalize on this potential, we create a new value conflict-focused CoT design that further smooths the sharpest direction of the loss landscape and increases moral reasoning performance. This finding shows that explicitly modifying and improving the design of reasoning dynamics offers a promising avenue for improving model performance on user requests with complex value conflicts, advancing pluralistic alignment in LLMs.

</details>


### [526] [Topological Signatures of Context-Level Reliability in TabPFN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17962)
*James Hu,Mahdi Ghelichi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TabPFN, a transformer-based model for tabular predictions, is evaluated for its internal representation behavior using zigzag persistent homology, revealing insights into its reliability across various synthetic tabular tasks with complex geometries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the internal behavior of TabPFN regarding its representation in difficult tabular geometries and its implications for model reliability.

Method: The study employs zigzag persistent homology to analyze the internal layer representations of TabPFN as evolving point clouds, using a controlled benchmark of synthetic tabular tasks featuring diverse topologies.

Result: Findings indicate a strong association between the geometry of TabPFN's internal representations and the reliability of its predictions; specific topological features correlate with various performance metrics such as Bayes error and mean absolute residuals.

Conclusion: Zigzag persistence serves as a diagnostic tool for assessing the reliability of TabPFN's inferred task geometry and can indicate when the model is operating under topologically challenging conditions.

Abstract: TabPFN is a transformer-based foundation model for tabular prediction that performs inference without task-specific training by conditioning on a support set and query inputs. Despite its strong empirical performance, its internal behavior on structurally difficult tabular geometries remains poorly understood. We study this behavior using zigzag persistent homology, treating TabPFN layer representations as evolving point clouds. We construct a controlled benchmark of synthetic tabular tasks with known true probabilities and varied intrinsic topology, including warped circles, tori, spheres, Hopf links, trefoil knots, and Swiss rolls. Across these tasks, we find that the topology of TabPFN's internal representation geometry is strongly associated with dataset-level reliability; for example, the zeroth homology group $H_0$ fragmentation count correlates positively with mean absolute residual across controlled tasks, and this association strengthens in a high-resolution warped circle case study at large sample size. Harder geometries induce a dual topological signature: increased $H_1$ loop activity and increased $H_0$ fragmentation, while the $H_1$ persistence becomes shorter-lived. These descriptors correlate with Bayes error, mean absolute residuals, and overconfidence. Our results suggest that zigzag persistence diagnoses the reliability of the inferred in-context task geometry and provides a context-level view of when TabPFN operates in topologically stressed regimes.

</details>


### [527] [DiFA: Inference-Time Forward-Process Alignment for Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17972)
*Shigui Li,Delu Zeng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DiFA introduces a training-free framework for diffusion model prediction that utilizes a sequential state estimation approach to enhance generative fidelity by addressing the limitations of numerical integration in inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
